water oak acorns are most astringent. None of these can be used raw, as human food, without more or less ill effect from the tannin con¬ tained. But there are tribes of western Indians who extract the tannin from even the most as¬ tringent acorns and make bread out of their flour. The process varies somewhat among different tribes, but essentially it as as follows: The acorns are collected when ripe, spread out to dry in the sun, cracked, and stored until the ker¬ nels are dry, care being taken that they do not mold. The kernels are then pulverized in a mortar to a fine meal, with frequent siftings to remove the coarser particles, until the whole is ground to a fine flour, this being essential. The tannin is then dis¬ solved out by placing the flour in a filter and let-

372 CAMPING AND WOODCRAF1 ting water percolate through it for about two hours, or until the water ceases to have a yellowish tinge. One form of filter is contrived by laying a coarse, flat basket or strainer on a pile of gravel with a drain underneath. Rather fine gravel is now scattered thickly over the bottom and up the sides of the strainer, and the meal laid thickly over the gravel. Water is added, little by little, to set free the tannin. The meal is removed by hand as much as possible, then water is poured over the remainder to get it together, and thus little is wasted. The meal by this time has the consistency of ordinary dough. The dough is cooked is two ways: first, by boiling it in water as we do corn-meal mush, the resulting porridge being not unlike yellow corn-meal mush in appearance and taste; it is sweet and wholesome, but rather insipid. The second mode is to make the dough into small balls, which are wrapped in green corn leaves. The sap season generally begins about the middle of March and lasts until the third week in April, but varies with a late or an early spring. It continues "good" from three to six weeks; that is, until the buds swell, after which the sap becomes strong and "buddy. . It flows best on a warm day succeeding a freezing night. Trees with large crowns yield the most sap. Those standing in or near cold springs discharge the most and sweetest sap. An average tree may yield, in favorable weather, about two gallons of sap in 24 hours. . , . , , The Indians' and early frontiersmen § method of

398 CAMPING AND WOODCRAFT tapping a tree was to "box" it by cutting a slanting notch in the trunk, about 8 inches long, two or three feet from the ground, and inserting an elder or sumac spout in the bark below the lower end of the notch, from which the sap was caught in a trough or pail; or, two gashes would be cut like a broad V, and a spout was put in at the bottom. Such notch¬ ing yields a rapid, flow, but spoils the tree. A better way is to bore a hole through the outer bark and just into the sapwood (say from one to two inches depth) on the sunny side of the tree, and insert a spout. With wooden spouts the hole must be larger than when iron ones are used, but make it no larger than necessary (certainly not over one inch), or you will injure the tree. The hole should slope slightly upward. Place a bucket under each spout. It may be necessary, in a wild region, to drive stout stakes around the buckets in such way that they cannot be robbed; for wild animals, as well as domestic ones, are inordinately

Skim this off, and continue the boil¬ ing until, (when a little of the sirup is stirred in a saucer, it grains (granulates); or until, when spread on the snow, it candies on cooling. Sap may be reduced to sugar by alternate freezing and thawing, the ice being thrown away each time it freezes. Just as good sugar and sirup are made from the red maple and from the silver (white or soft) maple as from the sugar maple (rock maple or sugar tree), but the sap is not quite so rich in sugar, and the running season is shorter. Since these trees bud earlier than sugar maple, they should be tapped earlier. The sap of the ash-leaved maple (com-

There is a decided maple flavor in the sap of the shellbark hickory. A good sirup can be concocted by steeping a handful of the dried and crushed inner bark of this tree in hot water to a strong "tea" and adding sufficient brown sugar. An extract com¬ mercially made from the bark is used in making a spurious "maple sirup" out of cane or corn sirup. It is safe to say that not one-tenth of the alleged maple sugar and sirup now on the market is free from this or similar adulteration. As a backwoods expedient, sirup may be made from the abundant and sugary sap of the black birch (sweet birch). In times of scarcity the pods of the honey locust have been utilized to the same end. They must be used within a month after maturity; later they become bitter. BEVERAGES None of our native plants contain principles that act upon the nerves like the caffein of coffee or the thein of tea; consequently all substitutes for coffee and tea are unsatisfying, except merely as hot drinks of agreeable taste. Millions of war-bound people are suffering this deprivation now. In the South, during the Civil War, many pitiful expedients were tried, such as decoctions of parched meal, dried sweet potatoes, wheat, chicory, cotton¬ seed, persimmon-seed, dandelion-seed, and the seeds of the Kentucky coffee-tree. Better substitutes for coffee were made from parched rye, from the seeds of the coffee senna (Cassia occidentalis) called "Magdad coffee," and from the parched and ground seeds of okra. Governor Brown of Georgia once said that the Confederates got more satisfaction out of the goldenrod flowers than out of any other makeshift for coffee. "Take the bloom," he dir¬ ected, "dry it, and boil to an extract" (meaning tincture). Teas, so-called, of very good flavor can be made from the dried root-bark of sassafras, or from its early buds, from the bark and leaves of spicewood,

4oo CAMPING AND WOODCRAFT from the leaves of chicory, ginseng, dittany, the sweet goldenrod (Solidago odora), and cinquefoil. Other plants used for the purpose are Labrador tea, Oswego tea, and (inferior) New Jersey tea. Our pioneers also made decoctions of chips of the arbor-vitae (white cedar) and of sycamore, the dried leaves of black birch, and the tips of hemlock boughs, sweetening them with maple sugar; but here we ap¬ proach the list of medicinal teas, which is well-nigh endless. The Indians made a really good "maple tea" by boiling sassafras-root bark for a short time in maple sap. Agreeable summer drinks can be made by infus¬ ing the sour fruit of the mountain ash (Pyrus Americana), from sumac berries (dwarf and stag'horn), and from the fruit of the red mulberry. The sweet sap of both hard and soft maples, box elder, and the birches (except red birch) is potable. Small beer can be made from the sap of black birch, from the pulp of honey locust pods, the fruit of the persimmon, shoots and root-bark of sassa¬ fras, and the twigs of black and red spruce. CHAPTER XXII LIVING OFF THE COUNTRY- IN EXTREMIS As I said at the beginning, the supreme test of woodcraft comes when the equipment has been destroyed by some disaster. Such misfortunes are not uncommon; if we seldom hear of them it is because they happen in far-away, isolated places, and the survivors are not interviewed by the press. A man gets lost and has to wander for a week, two weeks, or longer, before he meets a human being. A canoe is smashed to bits in a rapid, a hundred miles from the nearest outpost, and the men get ashore with nothing but the clothes they stand in and the contents of their pockets. And worse has happened. Robinson Crusoe had a pren¬ tice job compared to the actual experiences of hundreds of men and women whom fate has thrown, destitute of tools or weapons, far from the paths and courses of civilization. The pity is that such disasters befall, in so many cases, people who have no knowledge of how to meet them. Helplessness breeds despair. IN EXTREMIS.-The Far North is Famine Land, the world over, and to it we must look for examples of what men can subsist on when driven to the last extremity. In all northern countries, within the tree limit, it is customary, in starving times, to mix with the scanty hoard of flour the ground bark of trees. It is possible to support life even with bark alone. The Jesuit missionary Nicollet reported, more than two centuries ago, that an acquaintance of his, a French Indian-agent, lived seven weeks on bark alone, and the Relations of the order, in Canada, contain many instances of a like expedient. Those were hard times in New France! Such an experience as this was dismissed with a single sentence, quite as a matter of course: "An eelskin was deemed a sump¬ tuous supper; I had used one for mending a robe, but hunger obliged me to unstitch and eat it." Another brother says: "The bark of the oak, birch, linden, and that of other trees, when well cooked

deemed a sump¬ tuous supper; I had used one for mending a robe, but hunger obliged me to unstitch and eat it." Another brother says: "The bark of the oak, birch, linden, and that of other trees, when well cooked and pounded, and then put into the water in which fish had been boiled, or else mixed with fish-oil, made some excellent stews." Again: "they [the Indians] dried by a fire the bark of green oak, then they pounded it and made it into a porridge." It seems that the human stomach can stand a lot of tannin, if it has to do so. The young shoots of spruce and tamarack, the inner bark (in spring) of pine, spruce, and hemlock, young leaf-stems of beech, hickory and other trees, the buds of poplar, maple and wild rose, and the young leaves and flowers of basswood are nutritious; but these can be had only, of course, in spring. Far better than oak bark are the inner barks of alder, quaking aspen, basswood, birch, sweet bay, cotton¬ wood, slippery elm (this especially is nutritious),

LIVING OFF THE COUNTRY 421 white elm, pignut hickory, yellow locust, striped maple, poplar, and sassafras. The Chippewas boil the thick, sweetish bark of the shrubby bittersweet or staff-tree (Celastrus scandens) and use it for food. Young saplings of white cedar have a sweet pith of pleasant flavor which the Ojibways used in making soup. The following entry in the diary of Sir John Franklin sounds naive, when stripped of its context, but there is a world of grim pathos back of it: "There was no tripe de roche, so we drank tea and ate some of our shoes for supper." The rock tripe here referred to (Umbilicaria arctica or Dillenii) is one of several edible lichens that grow on rocks and are extensively used as human food in lands beyond the arctic tree limit. Reindeer moss (Cladonia rangiferina) and the* well-known Iceland moss (Cetraris Icelandica) are other examples. These are starchy, and, after being boiled for two or three hours, form a gelatinous mass that is digestible, though repulsive in appearance, one of the early Jesuits likening it to the slime of snails, and another admitting that "it is necessary to close one's eyes to eat it."

CHAPTER XXIII ACCIDENTS AND EMERGENCIES: THEIR BACKWOODS TREATMENT The present chapter is boiled down for the use of men of little or no surgical experience, who may suddenly find themselves wounded, or with an in¬ jured companion on their hands, when far away from any physician. In operating upon a comrade, the main things are to keep cool, act promptly, and make him feel that you have no doubt that you can pull him through all right. Place him in a comfortable position, and expose the wound. If you cannot otherwise remove the clothing quickly and without hurting him, rip it up the seam. First stop the bleeding, if there is any; then cleanse the wound of dirt (but do not wash it) ; then close it, if a cut or torn wound; then apply a sterilized dressing; then bandage it in place. Of course, if the injury is serious, you will immediately send a messenger hot-foot for a sur¬ geon, provided there is any chance of getting one. As for the patient himself, let him never say die. First-aid Materials.-Many of the operations hereinafter described can be performed with extem¬ porized materials; but antiseptics and sterilized dressings, ready at all times for instant use, are so essential in the treatment of wounds and other in¬ juries, that every wise traveler will carry on his person some sort of first-aid packet. Even if this be nothing more than one of the Red Cross dress¬ ings for small wounds and a few antiseptic tablets, sealed up in a waterproof and greaseproof envelope, which weighs practically nothing and takes up hard¬ ly any room, it may make all the difference between a quick cure and long suffering or death from bloodpoisoning. The pocket emergency case that I mentioned on page 103, along with a soldier s firstaid packet for major injuries, are sufficient to give emergency treatment in any case, yet the two to¬ gether weigh less than half a pound and can be carried in a coat pocket.

424 CAMPING AND WOODCRAFT Dressings.-Roller bandages are not recom¬ mended, save to men already trained to use them properly. Anybody, on the other hand, can apply the small ready-to-use Red Cross dressings, and adhesive plaster for strapping them on where they cannot be tied. For large wounds, the triangular bandage in a soldier's packet is easy for anyone to use, as there are cuts and directions printed on it showing how to apply it to any part of the person. A roll of adhesive plaster (zinc oxide plaster) is almost indispensable; but never apply it directly to a wound-first cover the hurt with a sterilized pad. Court plaster, although the commonest of first-aid dressings, is the poorest. It is likely to be surgically unclean, and has no antiseptic properties, but, on the contrary, it seals up the wound so as to confine whatever germs may have invaded it-the very worst thing it could do, for it defeats Nature in her effort to get rid of the poison by suppuration. Never turn a compress (or other dressing) over and use the other side; it is infected. Antiseptics.-Such dressings, however, are not enough in themselves to cleanse wounds and keep them free from infection. A supply of some good antiseptic is indispensable in the kit. Those com¬ monly used in domestic practice are either bulky liquids, impracticable on a "go-light" trip, or in¬ effective powders, like boric acid, that are only sooth¬ ing, not really germicidal. Mercury bichloride (corrosive sublimate) is a powerful agent, but it is so corrosive that it does not make fit solutions in metal vessels, which are all that a woodsman or explorer has. Besides, it is a deadly poison. Carbolic acid in solution is too bulky, and the full-strength liquid is mean to carry on a rough trip.

ACCIDENTS AND EMERGENCIES 425 Hitherto I have recommended iodine; but a bottle of it will make a sad mess of things if it leaks or breaks; an ampule in the pocket case serves for but one treatment, and, being in a wooden tube, is bulky in proportion. Iodine is poisonous, corrosive, painful in use, and impossible on delicate tissues. It has the further disadvantage that it clots blood serum, and so cannot penetrate a punctured wound unless the hole is slit open with a knife. Thanks to the discoveries of Dr. Carrel, with calcium hypochlorite, in the military hospitals of France, and of Dr. Dakin, who has produced a chlorine-carrier that does not deteriorate, we now have what seems to be the ideal antiseptic. I am at present using Dakin's antiseptic, as made here under the trade name of chlorazene. It is put up in tablet form. Chlorazene is neither poisonous nor corrosive in any marked degree. It can be employed, in proper solution, anywhere, even in the eye, as well as for sterilizing instruments and the hands of the operator. Yet it is one of the most powerful of all known antiseptics. Renew a large poultice every four or five hours, a small one every one or two hours. The woods themselves afford plenty of materials for good poultices. You may remember Leatherstocking (he was "Hawkejre" then) advising a wounded companion that "a little bruised alder will work like a charm." Saliva carries germs: so don't chew but bruise the leaves.

Bites of Other Animals.-Ordinarily the bite of a non-venomous animal needs no other attention than cleansing and an antiseptic dressing, unless there is enough laceration to require surgical meas¬ ures. Still, the bite of any animal, from mouse to man, may be dangerous. Germs from foul teeth may be carried into the wound. Vindictive and long-sustained anger sometimes seems to create a virus in the saliva, so that the bite of a teased and infuriated animal may act almost as a -venom. If there be reasonable doubt, cauterize the wound as for snake bite, or with nitrate of silver, or with a nail brought to a white heat (not so painful as if only red-hot). This will not, in all likihood, pre¬ vent an attack of hydrophobia if the animal was rabid, but it will kill such other poison or germs as may have been introduced. Not¬ withstanding that there are cranks (even a few of them in the medical profession) who assert that there is no such disease as rabies, it is in fact the most terrible ailment that afflicts mankind. In a great majority of cases, unless the patient is given the Pasteur treatment in due time, he will suffer the most excruciating agony, and death is certain, since no known drug is of any avail. Faith in the curative powers of "the madstone" is nothing but a superstition: the compacted fiber from an animal's stomach, or calculus, or porous stone, which goes by that name merely clings if there happens to be a discharge of blood or pus from the wound, and draws out no virus whatever; for there is none in the circulation-the virus of rabies travels along the nerves. Cleansing Wounds.-All inflammation of wounds, suppuration, abscesses, erysipelas, "bloodpoisoning," gangrene, and lockjaw, are due to liv¬ ing germs and nothing else. These germs are not born in the wound, but enter from the outside. We may as well say they are present everywhere, ex¬ cept in the air (pus germs do not float in air). To prevent their entrance is much easier than to kill them once they have gained foothold. The only guarantee of a wound healing nicely is to make and keep it surgically clean. Sterilize everything that is to be used about a wound: hands, instruments, and the dressing. Do not trust any¬ thing to be germ-free merely because it looks clean. The micro-organisms that cause inflammation of a wound, fever, putrefaction, may lurk anywhere,

452 CAMPING AND WOODCRAFT even in spotless linen fresh from the laundry, unless killed by antiseptics. Do not swab out a fresh wound, nor even wash it; that would only drive germs deeper in. Simply cover it with a sterilized dressing for the time being, and cleanse it later with an antiseptic wash, if need be. Plain water is likely to contain germs. If it is necessary first to pick out hard foreign matter that has been driven into the wound, do so with an instrument sterilized by heat or by antiseptics, or made from a freshly cut green stick. Whenever practicable, shave off the hair for some distance around the wound. Hairs, no mat¬ ter how small, are grease-coated and favor the lodg¬ ment and growth of germs. Shaving also scrapes off the surface dirt and dead scales of skin. Closing Wounds.-Never cover a wound with court plaster. It prevents the free escape of sup¬ puration, inflames the part, and makes the place difficult to cleanse thereafter. If the clothing catches fire, lie down and roll over slowly, beating out the fire with the hands or smothering it with earth. When rescuing another person whose clothing is aflame, throw him down and do the same, or wrap him as tightly as possible in a blanket, coat, or the like, leaving only his head out. Woolens do not burn with a flame like cot¬ ton and linen. Frostbite, Freezing.-In extreme cold, let each member of a party watch the others for the white spots that denote frostbite. These should be rub¬ bed with a woolen mitten or glove, rather than snow. If the freezing is severe, so that the tissues are stiff, rough rubbing and twisting may break them. The return to warmth must be gradual, as a sudden reaction is dangerous to the vitality of the parts. Keep out in the cold, rub the frozen surface gently with snow, or ice-water, until the natural color of the skin is restored. To toast frost-bitten fingers or toes before a fire

is dangerous to the vitality of the parts. Keep out in the cold, rub the frozen surface gently with snow, or ice-water, until the natural color of the skin is restored. To toast frost-bitten fingers or toes before a fire would at least bring chilblains, and thawing out rapidly a badly frozen part would result in gan¬ grene, making amputation necessary. When cir¬ culation is restored, rub with kerosene, whiskey, or alcohol and water. This will keep the skin from peeling off. In case the frostbite is old and blackened, or the skin has begun to slough off, treat it just as you would a burn. When in danger of freezing to death, compel yourself to keep awake and moving. If there are two or more of you, beat each other unmercifully with sticks. To sleep is death. Do not drink liq¬ uor: the reaction from it is likely to be fatal. In rescuing one who is almost insensible from cold, take him into a cold room. Rub his limbs toward the body to restore circulation, first with rough cloths wet in cold water, then in warmer and warmer water, finally with alcohol and water.

Ivy Poisoning (Poison Oak, Poison Sumac).- We have three species of plants that secrete an oil which poisons human beings (no other animals) by contact. Most virulent of these is the poison sumac or "poison elder" (Rhus vernix), which is distinguished from other sumacs by bearing a white fruit like thin clusters of very small grapes, and by its leaf, the edge of which is smooth instead of notched. The so-called poison ivy (Rhus toxicodendron) is readily told from the harmless Virginia creeper by having three leaves, instead of five, and from the wild bean vine by its lack of conspicuous flowers

The latter name should be reserved for Rhus diversiloba, which does not grow east of the Rocky Mountains. All three of these plants are really sumacs, notwithstanding that the "ivy" creeps on the ground, or climbs trees, walls, or fences, like a true vine. When poison ivy is in bloom, the spores of its pollen are blown hither and yon by every breeze, and those minute spores bear some of the poisonous oil that makes the plant an enemy of the human race. That is why people who are particularly susceptible may be poisoned if they go within ten feet of the plant. The poison is of an acid nature; consequently if one rubs his skin with an alkali (such as baking soda, weak ammonia, soap, or wood ashes) before hand¬ ling the plant, or immediately after doing so, he will be uninjured. North Cascades National Park There are countless backcountry routes and possibilities in this wild land. The diversity of climate and geography creates very different habitats on the west and east side of the crest, as well as fostering a great array of plants and animals. Cascading water is fed by over 300 glaciers and countless snowfields. Lakes are abundant. Almost 400 miles (644km) of trails, mostly in major drainages and over high passes, traverse this tremendous landscape. Your path may follow a route used for many centuries by people who have long crossed these mountains or sought food and resources here, or you may venture to an area so wild it feels as if you are the first explorer. Wilderness Information Center Open seasonally (May - October) When to Visit Low elevation trails are most visited between April and October, with the driest weather from mid-June to September. Visitation to the high country (above 5,000 ft/ 1524 m) is greatest after the snows melt, generally from July through early October. The best snow mountaineering conditions are often June and July. The park is open year round, but heavy winter precipitation limits road access and increases backcountry hazards between November and March. How Large Is Your Group? Permits Are Limited To protect the wilderness and visitors' experiences, the number of permits issued for each area is limited. Popular areas such as around Cascade Pass, along Ross Lake, on Copper Ridge, and at Thornton and Monogram Lakes can be very busy during the height of summer, and permits can fill quickly. The busiest climbing areas are: Sulphide Glacier, Boston Basin, and Eldorado cross-country zones. To maximize your chance of obtaining a permit and finding solitude, visit these areas midweek or after Labor Day, and have a backup itinerary or climb in mind if your first-choice area is already full. Ask a ranger for less busy alternative areas to visit. There is always somewhere to go. Why do I need a permit? Backcountry permits protect your wilderness experience by preventing overcrowding at camps or climbing routes, and protecting natural resources so all visitors, including future generations, can enjoy them. Permits also serve an important safety function during emergencies and wildfires, and allow managers to gather data for decision making. Traveling with Pack Animals Pack animals (horses, mules, burros or llamas) are allowed on a variety of stock trails and at stock camps,as trail conditions permit. Some trails are closed to stock. Stock may also travel cross-country on the eastern side of the park around Rainbow, Boulder, and Fourmile Creeks. Note that all party size limits apply to people and stock combined. Grazing (with permit) is allowed in some parts of the recreation areas,but not in the national park- carry weed-free hay or pellet feed instead. Hikers should yield the right of way to all stock, and speak softly with the riders about how to proceed. For more information on stock use, contact the Wilderness Information Center. Fishing There are a variety of native and non-native fish in the park's lakes and streams. Although many creeks run too fast to provide good fishing, many of the lakes have ample, if small, fish. Fishing is allowed in accordance with Washington State Law and with a state fishing license. Obtain your license before arriving at the park, as they are not available at ranger stations. Many lakes are high elevation and do not allow campfires. Plan to fry your catch over a campstove, and dispose of fish entrails in deep water, fast streams, or scattered widely over an area far from any camps. in Weather Although the North Cascades frequently enjoy a summer drought with warm, dry conditions, cool rainy weather is a possibility year-round, and higher elevations are colder. Snow is possible in any month, especially at the higher elevations and early or late season. Check the forecast before leaving home,but remember that the weather in the North Cascades can change quickly. Even in the summer, warm layers and good rain gear are a necessity, and a hat and gloves are often welcome. Dress in layers so you can regulate your body temperature by adding or removing insulation. Avoid cotton clothing-it is cold and does not insulate well when wet. Instead, bring wool, fleece or other synthetics, which perform much better in wet or cool conditions. Safety in the Subalpine Environment With a few notable exceptions, most trails typically follow valley bottoms to high passes, as the terrain is usually too steep to follow high ridges. Trails over alpine passes tend to be quite steep, so plan your daily mileage estimates with this in mind. Travel over steep snow requires sturdy boots, an ice axe and knowledge of how to self-arrest on steep slopes. There are no trail markers or blazes, so snow cover can make route-finding a challenge. Cross in the morning before snow melt swells the water level. Mountaineering Safety The numerous peaks and glaciers of the North Cascades present a variety of challenges and rewards for the mountaineer: classic mixed mountaineering routes, glacier travel, technical rock climbing, and scrambling, all within a premier wilderness setting. If you are new to the sport, join a club or take a class to learn more about the challenges, risks, and rewards of this activity,including proper instruction on the equipment and skills you need to stay safe. The Wilderness Information Center has climbing rangers on hand to assist you in planning your climb. Plan Ahead and Prepare Be informed about the area, including local weather, trail conditions, and regulations. Choose destinations that your group is physically in condition to handle, and know your group's limits. Visiting in small groups (four to six)gives you more flexibility and has less impact. Learn the necessary skills and know how to use your gear before you head into the wilderness, especially if you will be crossing steep snow, traveling cross-country, or mountaineering. Travel and Camp on Durable Surfaces Along trail corridors: Camp only in designated camps (marked by name posts) along trails, in the location specified on your backcountry permit. Pitch your tent on established bare sites, not the vegetation. Protect the native vegetation and reduce erosion by staying on the trail, even if it's muddy. Traveling Cross-country: Cross-country camping is allowed for those who are up to the challenge of off-trail travel. Seek a route over rock or snow, or spread your group out to avoid creating a trail through vegetation. Dispose of Waste Properly Use toilets where provided. Pit or composting toilets are located at most designated campsites. If there is no toilet, walk at least 200 feet (63 m) from camp or water, and dig a small "cat hole" about six to eight inches (15 to 20cm) deep. Leave plants, rocks and artifacts as you find them, so that others may discover and enjoy them. Avoid altering your site: Digging out rocks, moving logs, building windbreaks or trenching all disturb the natural area. Leave the land as you found it. Edible fruits and berries may be gathered for personal consumption (1 liter per day). Mushroom collecting is not allowed. Minimize Campfire Impacts Camp stoves are recommended for all cooking. They are clean, light, efficient and don't scar the land or deplete natural wood sources. Fires are not allowed at some camps, including those in the subalpine, nor in any cross-country areas. Where fires are allowed, build a small, lowimpact fire in an existing firepit at an established camp. Burn only small pieces of dead and downed wood that fit entirely within the firepit. Be sure the fire is dead out before leaving. Try these alternatives to an evening fire: bring

in an existing firepit at an established camp. Burn only small pieces of dead and downed wood that fit entirely within the firepit. Be sure the fire is dead out before leaving. Try these alternatives to an evening fire: bring a candle lantern, or bring a star chart and identify constellations. Respect Wildlife Many animals are attracted by food smells, strong odors, and salt. Seeking food from humans and loss of natural wariness are harmful to wildlife. Many bears (mostly black, but grizzlies are possible) make their home in the North Cascades, and sightings are not uncommon. Deer, mountain goats, marmots and other rodents are attracted to the salt in urine and sweat, and they have chewed or ruined unattended gear, clothing, and boots. Help protect yourself,your gear, and all wildlife by following these requirements and tips: Store all food and scented items properly. Bears learn quickly and return to areas where they obtain food. This can be unhealthy for the bear and problematic for you or the next visitor. To secure your food from wildlife, you will need a waterproof sack dedicated to smelly food and garbage storage,plus at least 50 feet (15m) of lightweight cord. Hang the stuff

Hang the stuff sack with food,cooking gear, garbage, and any other scented items at least 15 feet (4.6m)from the ground and 5 feet (1.5m) out from the limb and tree trunk. Since trees with large limbs are not always present, this technique can require time and ingenuity. Avoid trampling fragile vegetation in your search for a tree. Use an animal resistant food storage canister. This is an excellent alternative to a food hang or for use in areas where trees are limited. The Wilderness Information Center loans out canisters free of charge, as do other ranger stations. Canisters are required in some areas. Keep a clean camp and minimize smells. Establish a cooking area well away from your sleeping and food storage areas, and keep tents, clothing and sleeping bags clean and free of food scents. Seal all leftovers and garbage in plastic bags and secure with your food away from wildlife. Whenever possible, sleep at least 100 yards (91 m) away from food storage and cooking areas. Never bury or burn leftovers or trash, or throw them in the toilets-the smell will linger and attract rodents or bears. Leave pets at home. They can disrupt native wildlife or get injured or lost. Many hikers wish to enjoy natural surroundings without interference from domestic animals. Pets are prohibited in the National Park-be sure you know where your trail takes you. Enjoy wildlife from a distance-never approach or feed a bear or any other wild animal. Report all bear and other unusual wildlife sightings or interactions to the nearest ranger station. Congress has designated 94% of the Complex as the Stephen Mather Wilderness. The Stephen Mather Wilderness is at the heart of over two million acres of some of the wildest lands remaining-a place "where the earth and its community of life are untrammeled by man...." Untrammeled (meaning"free of restraint," "unconfined") captures the essence of wilderness: a place where the land's natural processes prevail, and the developments of modern technological society are largely unnoticeable. Here, we are visitors, but we also come home-to our natural heritage. It is a place to experience our past and a place to find future respite. This is the enduring legacy of

TC 3-97.61 MILITARY MOUNTAINEERING NOVEMBER 2025 DISTRIBUTION RESTRICTION: Approved for public release; distribution is unlimited. This publication supersedes TC 3-97.61, dated 26 July 2012. HEADQUARTERS, DEPARTMENT OF THE ARMY
This publication is available at the Army Publishing Directorate site (https://armypubs.army.mil) and the Central Army Registry Site (https://atiam.train.army.mil/catalog/dashboard).

Preface TC 3-97.61 is the Army's doctrinal publication for military mountaineering. It provides doctrinal guidance and direction for how U.S. forces train military mountaineers to operate in complex and mountainous terrain. This training circular is designed to work in conjunction with and complement ATP 3-21.50 and ATP 3-90.97. This manual enables leaders and Soldiers to understand mountain and cold-weather environments; their effects on personnel, operations, and equipment; and most importantly, how units train Soldiers to prepare to deploy in complex mountain environments. The principle audience for this publication is all members of the profession of arms. Introduction Operating in a mountainous environment is a continual exercise in problem solving and critical thinking. This document presents proven, utilitarian techniques for approaching the mountain and cold-weather problem issues. This training circular should not be interpreted as prescriptive in nature but rather a starting place and solid reference for best practices and risk mitigation. There is no substitute for experience and practice when dealing with mountainous environments. As the old adage goes, "There are bold climbers and there are old climbers. There are no bold old climbers." Chapter 1 Mountain Environment Around the world, mountain ranges form natural borders and boundaries. Historically, they have formed the edge of human settlement and wilderness; today, mountains still define many national borders and conflict regions. Mountain environments are demanding and tough, with conditions that interfere with all warfighting functions. To fight in the complex terrain of mountainous regions, military mountaineers must become familiar with the significant challenges that this environment presents. This rugged terrain will prove to be an overwhelming challenge to the untrained and inexperienced Soldier. Military mountaineers must understand how mountain environment characteristics affect them, the mission, their equipment, and the enemy during military operations. Rough terrain slows movements and canalizes troops into narrow corridors. Steep slopes make vehicle traffic possible only on roads that require extensive engineering and are vulnerable to attack and natural hazards, such as rockslides and avalanches. Harsh weather limits air resupply and close air support. Radio communications can only be maintained by securing exposed ridge tops. Key terrain often requires significant effort to secure and an even larger commitment to sustain. To succeed in this environment, Soldiers must be prepared mentally and physically. Mountain Environment DEFINITION: TYPES AND FORMATIONS OF MOUNTAINS 1-2. Mountains are landforms that rise more than 500 meters above the surrounding plain and are characterized by steep slopes. They may rise abruptly from the plains to form a giant barrier or ascend gradually as a series of parallel ridges extending unbroken for great distances. Cliffs and precipices may be near vertical or even overhanging. Mountains may have isolated peaks, rounded crests, eroded ridges, and high plains. They may be cut by valleys, gorges, and deep ravines. High rocky crags with glaciated peaks and year-round snow-cover exist in mountain ranges at most latitudes along the western portion of the Americas, in Europe, and in Asia. MOUNTAIN BUILDING 1-3. Understanding the processes and the conditions under which mountains form helps us to understand their structures and hazards. The two primary mechanisms for mountain building are volcanic and tectonic activity. Volcanoes are constructed from lava and ash, which begin within the earth as magma. Tectonic activity causes plates to collide, heaving up fold mountains, or to pull apart and crack, forming fault-block mountain ranges. TYPICAL MOUNTAIN STRUCTURES 1-4. The massive slabs composing the outer layer of the earth are called tectonic plates. Their

The massive slabs composing the outer layer of the earth are called tectonic plates. Their movement relative to each other creates earthquakes, volcanoes, ocean trenches, and mountain ridge systems. The different horizontal and vertical stresses that create mountains usually produce complex patterns. Each type of stress produces a typical structure, and most mountains can be described in terms of the following structures: * Dome mountains-a simple, upward bulge of the crust forms dome mountains. They are usually the result of the upward movement of magma and the folding of the rock layers overhead. Erosion may strip away the overlying layers, exposing the central igneous core. * Fault-block mountains-faulting, or cracking of the crust into large chunks, often accompanies upwarp, a broad low arching of the surface, which results in fault-block mountains. The motion of chunks along these faults creates various forms of mountains. * Fold mountains-tectonic forces, in which continental plates collide or ride over each other, have given rise to the most common mountain form: fold mountains. When erosion strips down the overburden of rock from folded mountain ranges, the oldest, central core is all that remains. * Volcanic mountains-along convergent plate boundaries, volcanic activity increases. Erosion is when precipitation scours soil and loose rock from the steep slopes of mountains. Cycles of freeze-thaw exert tremendous force in cracks and fissures in the rock. These forces break apart softer rock and wash the fragments away down creeks and drainages, forming many of the gullies and smaller terrain features on the mountains. 1-7. Glaciation is when glaciers are rivers of ice and rocks that slowly move down mountains. They form when the rate of snowfall exceeds the rate of melting in summer months. After accumulations over hundreds of years, the snow compresses into ice that can range from ten to several hundred feet thick. Chapter 1 TERRAIN FEATURES AND TERMS 1-8. Common geologic terminology includes- * Summit, peak-the highest point. * Spire-a tall, narrow rock formation, resembling a steeple. * Ridge-a line of high ground with height variations along its crest. * Valley-low ground bordered on the sides by higher ground. A valley may or may not contain a stream course. A valley generally has maneuver room within its confines. * Hanging valley-a valley whose lower end is high on a sheer wall of a larger valley into which it flows. * Saddle-a dip or low point along the crest of a ridge. A saddle is not necessarily the lower ground between two hilltops; it may be a break along an otherwise level ridge crest. * Pass-any route from one valley over higher ground to another valley. Usually, a relatively low point along a ridge. Many regional synonyms exist to describe pass, such as the word notch in New England. * Col-the low point on a ridge joining two peaks. Glaciologists reserve this term for gaps of glacial origin, but others use it much more generally. * Cirque-a bowl-shaped valley high on a mountain, usually of glacial origin. Higher in the mountains, soil depth and quality deteriorate, and conditions become too harsh for trees. Slopes with enough soil are often covered with grass tussocks and low shrubs. Where soil is washed away, there is only exposed rock. Rock comes in many forms and is classified by origin and mineral composition: * Igneous rocks-igneous rocks form from cooled magma. The two main categories are intrusive and extrusive: Plutonic (intrusive) rocks-slow crystallization from deeply buried magmas generally means good climbing, since the minerals formed are relatively large and interwoven into a solid matrix. Weathering develops protrusions of resistant minerals, which make for either a rough-surfaced rock with excellent friction or, if the resistant crystals are much larger than the surrounding matrix, a surface with numerous knobby holds. Granite-granite is a very hard rock and provides good climbing. It produces less rockfall than softer rock, but when rock breaks away, it may be as large boulders. After a rain, granite dries quickly. Most protection is found in cracks. Face climbing can be found; however, it is not easily protected. Scree refers to small rocks, from pebble size to dinner-plate size. It accumulates in areas abundant with weak, brittle rock. These small stones do not settle into stable slopes. Climbing scree is inefficient because it is unstable, with each step sliding down as weight is placed upon it. Firmer footing may be found around the edge of rock outcroppings. Scree can be descended quickly by sliding on one's feet but should be done so under control. TALUS 1-19. Talus refers to rocks larger than a dinner plate but smaller than boulders. They can be used as steppingstones to ascend or descend a slope. The stability of talus can vary. Mountain Environment KEY AND DECISIVE TERRAIN 1-36. Mountain warfare is a fight to control roads, and the lines of communication (LOCs) located in valleys. Controlling them enables the movement of road-bound critical supplies and heavy combat assets, such as tanks that must transit through the mountains to other fronts of the battlefield. The decisive terrain for control of these LOCs is often the passes. Here, the valleys narrow and rise, limiting the maneuver of armor and mechanized units. The terrain canalizes these forces into terrain dominated by the surrounding heights. Here, these assets experience degradation of their maneuver and firepower capability, making them vulnerable to attacks from mobile and light mountain infantry forces. The unit that holds this decisive terrain can protect its own heavy assets as it moves through mountainous terrain and destroys enemy assets attempting to take the same route. 1-37. The high ground offers a tactical advantage to whoever holds it. In the valley, cover shrinks when engaged from an elevated position. On the heights, even relatively small cover gives protection from direct fires from the valley and using ridge crests allows units to maneuver while masked by terrain. However, the tactical advantage of holding high ground

Changes in atmospheric pressure are the underlying cause of many factors. Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the atmosphere in an area. As elevation increases, pressure is reduced, causing lower air density. Aircraft capabilities and human performance decrease. Sunlight is less filtered, causing quicker warming and cooling. 1-56. Reduced pressure also affects temperature. Air temperature decreases as elevation increases in the mountains at the adiabatic rate or about 3 degrees (°) Fahrenheit (F) to 5 °F for every 1,000 feet of elevation gain. Cooler air holds less moisture. As air masses pass over mountains, they are lifted by the terrain-a process known as orographic lift. If the air cools to its saturation temperature, its water vapor condenses and becomes a visible cloud. Chapter 1 CLOUDS 1-74. At the boundaries of major weather systems where different air masses collide, warm air is lifted into the atmosphere, causing clouds and precipitation. Fronts create distinctive cloud formations. Warm fronts, where the incoming warm air gradually displaces cold air below, present as steadily thickening and lowering clouds over a few days. Cold fronts create an uplift that is more violent and may come as a single, larger storm system. High-Level Clouds 1-75. High-level clouds (above 6,000 meters) are formed of ice crystals, with a fibrous structure and blurred outlines. The sky is often covered with a thin veil that partly obscures the sun or, at night, produces a ring of light around the moon. Cirrus clouds indicate moisture aloft and the approach of a traveling storm system. Precipitation is often 24 to 36 hours away. As a storm approaches, the high-level clouds thicken and lower. Mid-Level Clouds 1-76. Mid-level clouds (2,000 to 6,000 meters) appear more distinct than high-level clouds because of a mixed composition of water droplets and ice. Mid-level clouds often form in advance of a cold front. Puffy, mid-level clouds on a warm, humid summer morning are commonly followed by thunderstorms later in

Puffy, mid-level clouds on a warm, humid summer morning are commonly followed by thunderstorms later in the day. "Fair weather" cumulus are clouds scattered rather than even in a blue sky and suggest arrival of high pressure and clear skies. Low-Level Clouds 1-77. Low-level clouds (below 2,000 meters) are mostly composed of water droplets. Most precipitation originates from low-level clouds because rain or snow usually evaporates before reaching the ground from higher clouds. Low-level clouds usually indicate impending precipitation. Vertical Development (Cumulonimbus) 1-78. Large, vertical development clouds often form on the steep, leading edge of a cold front. They can develop as individual towers or form a line of towers called a squall line. Their formation is fueled by vigorous convective updrafts. Chapter 2 Training Military Mountaineers Operational success in complex, compartmentalized, and objectively hazardous terrain largely rests on the shoulders of a unit's military mountaineers. Often, these are the only unit members with significant experience living and moving in mountainous terrain. Units with highly experienced mountaineers and well-developed mountain programs will be better prepared to engage in mountain warfare and will likely prove more successful. Military mountaineers serve as advisors for the development of such programs and trainers for mountain knowledge and skills; they also ensure safe training conduct in hazardous terrain. Chapter 3 Environmental Injuries Operations in mountainous areas will expose Soldiers to a variety of harsh environmental conditions not found in lowland areas. Soldiers exposed to these conditions are at a heightened risk of becoming a casualty. This risk increases with lack of experience and training. Troops conducting operations in mountainous regions often encounter cold temperatures that can degrade physical performance, impact morale, and create cold-weather casualties. The lack of oxygen in high-altitude environments impairs many aspects of normal Soldier tasks. Soldiers may develop altitude illnesses that can produce debilitating symptoms and require immediate MEDEVAC. If not accounted for in the planning process, these conditions will negatively impact the mission. Soldiers will become fatigued sooner in this environment and must reduce their pace or lighten their load to remain healthy and effective. With experience and proper training, Soldiers will become more durable and lethal in this environment. SECTION I - ENVIRONMENTAL INJURY PREVENTION 3-1. A Soldier needs about 3 to 6 liters of water each day to prevent dehydration when living and performing physical labor in a cold or mountainous environment. Leaders should monitor their Soldiers' water intake, since motivation to drink cold water in a cold environment is low. Coffee and tea are diuretics and cause excessive urination, which contributes to dehydration. They should be avoided. However, providing other noncaffeinated hot liquids is a good way to encourage Soldiers to drink more water. The adequacy of liquid intake can best be judged by the color of urine and volume. Dark, amber-colored urine instead of light yellow or the absence of a need to urinate upon awakening from a night's sleep is an indicator of dehydration. Thirst is not a good indicator of hydration. Factors that contribute to dehydration in cold weather are- * The thirst mechanism does not function properly in cold weather. * Water is often inconvenient to obtain and purify. * The air in cold climates and at high altitudes lacks moisture. * Cold causes frequent urination. Symptoms of dehydration include darkening urine, decreased amounts of urine being produced, dry mouth, tiredness, mental sluggishness, lack of appetite, headache, fainting, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, higher temperature, upset stomach, and unconsciousness. The symptoms of dehydration resemble those of hypothermia. To distinguish between them, open the victim's clothes and feel the stomach. If the stomach is cold, the victim is probably hypothermic; if it is warm, the victim is probably dehydrated. This can contribute to dehydration, which is the precursor to several other cold-weather injuries, both freezing and non-freezing. Treatment 3-8. Chapter 3 Sunburn 3-23. Excessive UV radiation from sunlight is a serious threat to military personnel operating in high mountain regions during daylight hours because of several factors increasing its damaging potential. UV exposure can cause significant short-term disability to military personnel through severe sunburn. Contributing Factors 3-24. Decreased UV filtering by the thinner atmosphere at high altitude causes an increased intensity of exposure (approximately 4 percent for every 1,000 feet of elevation increase) and a shift of the UV spectrum to more harmful short wavelengths. Reflection from snow and ice increases the intensity of exposure (approximately 75 percent of incident radiation is reflected). Soldiers vary greatly in their risk of sunburn based on their skin type and pigment. Symptoms 3-25. Symptoms of sunburn are painful, burning, red, or blistered skin with slight swelling. Chapter 3 TYPES 3-40. Cold injuries may be divided into two types: freezing and non-freezing. The freezing type is known as frostbite. The nonfreezing type includes hypothermia, chilblain, and immersion foot. Cold injuries result from impaired circulation and from cold and ice forming upon the tissues of the body. Temperature alone is not a reliable guide as to whether a cold injury can occur. Low temperatures are necessary for cold injuries to occur, but freezing temperatures are not. Wind speed can accelerate body heat loss under both wet and cold conditions. PREVENTATIVE MEASURES 3-41. Commanders should ensure the following measures are taken to prevent cold-weather injuries: * Soldiers' uniforms are kept as dry as possible and are protected from the elements. * Soldiers are educated on proper use of clothing systems to avoid the effects of overheating and perspiration (layer dressing and ventilation). * The buddy system is used to watch for early signs of cold-weather injuries. * All Soldiers waterproof their equipment. * The rate of movement should be slow, deliberate, and careful. Soldiers should not move out at a force march pace and then be stationary after they have perspired heavily. Soldiers should not wear excessive cold-weather clothing

Several demographic, behavioral, and past history characteristics increase risk for cold-weather injuries. Body Composition 3-43. Individuals with a high amount of body surface area relative to their body mass (long and lean) lose more body heat in the cold than individuals with a small surface area relative to their body weight (short and stocky) do. The reason for this is that the principal means of heat loss in the cold is at the skin surface. This effect is somewhat reduced in short, stocky people because a large body mass maintains a constant temperature better than a small body mass. Sex 3-44. The peripheral (for example, hands and feet) cold-injury rate for female Soldiers is two times higher than the rate for males. Sex differences during cold exposure are almost entirely attributable to women's generally greater body fat content and thicker fat layer under the skin compared to men of comparable age and weight. times higher than the rate for males. Sex differences during cold exposure are almost entirely attributable to women's generally greater body fat content and thicker fat layer under the skin compared to men of comparable age and weight. Women typically have a greater surface area but smaller total body mass (thus lower total body heat content) than men do. Race 3-45. African-American male and female Soldiers are two to four times more likely to suffer a cold-weather injury versus their Caucasian counterparts. This increased risk is consistent across all career management fields, which suggests that occupational exposure does not account for the differences between African-Americans and Caucasians. Differences between races may be due to cold-weather experience, but more likely they are due to anthropomorphic considerations (longer, thinner digits) and perhaps greater surface-area-to-mass ratio. Fitness and Training 3-46. Overall, physical training and fitness levels appear to have only minor influences on cold management. Fitter individuals can sustain more physical activity at a higher intensity and longer duration; therefore, they produce more heat from exercise for longer periods when compared to less fit individuals. 30 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Environmental Injuries Fatigue 3-47. Physical fatigue can impair shivering and peripheral vasoconstriction responses during cold exposure. Therefore, physical fatigue can increase the Soldier's risk for hypothermia. Fatigued Soldiers cannot sustain sufficient activity levels to maintain body temperature during severe cold exposure. Age 3-48. Soldiers who are 45 years of age or older may be less cold tolerant than younger people, either because of a decline in physical fitness or because of reduced vasoconstriction and heat conservation in comparison to their younger counterparts. Dehydration 3-49. Dehydration can increase susceptibility to cold injury by decreasing the ability to sustain physical activity (particularly if accompanied by heat stress from exercising in heavy clothing) and, therefore, decreasing the ability to sustain thermal balance. In addition, dehydration might impair cognitive function and cause Soldiers to use poor judgment. Dehydration has not been shown to reduce peripheral skin temperatures and does not impair shivering. Sustained Operations 3-50. Exertional fatigue, sleep restriction, and underfeeding are common stressors during sustained operations and together impair a Soldier's ability to maintain thermal balance in the cold. The metabolic heat production response degrades and impairs the ability to sustain exercise performance. Soldiers engaged in sustained operations also may make more judgment

during sustained operations and together impair a Soldier's ability to maintain thermal balance in the cold. The metabolic heat production response degrades and impairs the ability to sustain exercise performance. Soldiers engaged in sustained operations also may make more judgment errors when tired and increase their exposure and risk of injury. A given cold stressor is more likely to induce cold injury after a long period of sustained operations compared to earlier in the operation. This emphasizes the need for planned rest, sleep, feeding, and recovery before conducting stressful operations in the cold. Food and Nutrient Consumption 3-51. Consuming too little nutrients can result in hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), which can impair shivering. Hypoglycemia contributes to an inability to sustain physical activity and the associated exercise-induced heat production during cold exposure. In addition, alcohol blunts the senses and impairs judgment, so the Soldier may not feel the signs and symptoms of a developing cold injury. Soldiers must not consume alcohol while exposed to cold weather. Nicotine 3-53. Smoking or chewing tobacco can increase susceptibility to frostbite by increasing vasoconstriction in the periphery (for example, the hands). Frostbite is the freezing or crystallization of living tissues due to heat being lost faster than it can be replaced by blood circulation or from direct exposure to extreme cold or high winds. Once the foot is rewarmed, it will swell and putting the boot back on will not be possible. SECTION II - ALTITUDE EFFECTS, INJURIES, AND ACCLIMATIZATION 3-76. As altitude increases, the overall atmospheric pressure decreases. Decreased pressure is the underlying source of altitude illnesses. Whether at sea level or 20,000 feet, the surrounding atmosphere has the same percentage of oxygen. As pressure decreases, the body has a much more difficult time passing oxygen from the lungs to the red blood cells and thus to body tissues. Chapter 4 Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment Units receiving mountain training show a marked advantage in harsh mountain environments than those that do not. Normal activities, such as navigating, communicating, and moving, require specialized techniques. To gain confidence and experience, Soldiers must conduct realistic mountain training. They should be expected to perform under any environmental conditions. Extended training exercises test the sustainment mechanisms in place for the unit and expose the Soldier to the isolation common to mountain operations. Training should reflect the harsh mountain environment and should focus on the following: * Fitness and nutrition. * Ability to survive and operate in a cold-weather environment. * Resupply methods. * Soldier load management. * Bivouac considerations. The clothing system refers to every piece of clothing placed against the skin (base layer), the insulating layers, and the outermost garments (shell), which protect the Soldier from the elements. When clothing is worn properly, the Soldier can function better; when clothing is worn improperly, Soldiers can develop hypothermia or frostbite. Wearing cold-weather clothing provides a barrier against weather and heat retention, moves moisture away from skin, dries quickly, and allows for adequate dexterity. 4-31. Clothing for the cold-weather environment must manage Soldiers' temperatures and control moisture. Clothing must be able to vent and breathe so a Soldier does not become overheated and perspire excessively. The clothing must also create insulation to shelter the Soldier from extreme temperatures. Clothing must manage moisture that comes from external sources, such as rain, or from internal sources, such as perspiration. 4-32. One of the most effective ways to manage moisture from perspiration is to set a pace that limits exertion. In a cold-weather environment, patrols should move at a pace that will not saturate Soldiers' insulating layers with sweat. Rest halts allow Soldiers an opportunity to adjust layers and control their own individual temperatures. 4-33. Fitness, load, body composition, and metabolism all affect individual clothing needs. There should be room for individual variation in the wear of cold-weather clothing, but clothing decisions should be based on the principles of moisture management, trapped air spaces, and protection from the elements. The components of any clothing system can be broken down into the following general categories to match those principles. BASE LAYER 4-34. The base layer is a thin, lightweight moisture-wicking layer worn against skin and moves moisture away from the skin to prevent heat loss from conduction. Base layers should be constructed of wool, synthetic, or silk fabrics. INSULATING LAYERS 4-35. Insulating layers are those layers worn over the base layer and under the shell. Insulating layers provide additional warmth by resisting the transfer of heat. Modern

Base layers should be constructed of wool, synthetic, or silk fabrics. INSULATING LAYERS 4-35. Insulating layers are those layers worn over the base layer and under the shell. Insulating layers provide additional warmth by resisting the transfer of heat. Modern insulating layers allow moisture to move easily, and they trap air to increase the insulating factor. Several thin layers of insulation provide more warmth than one thick layer. Insulating layers should be constructed from wool, synthetic, or down fabrics. Insulating layers help Soldiers retain heat and not lose heat through convection. SHELL 4-36. The shell is the outermost layer worn. The shell is the primary barrier between the elements and the body and prevents outside moisture from getting in, while allowing inside moisture out. Shells must have some ventilation capacity to prevent overheating. There are two types of shells. 4-37. A hard shell is generally more moisture and wind repellant and provides better protection against the elements at the cost of breathability. Soldiers cannot ventilate their bodies as well with a hard shell. The hard shell is a good outer layer to be worn in extreme conditions or static environments. 4-38. Operations in mountainous terrain require Soldiers to carry only mission-essential items as they move through challenging terrain. Individual Soldiers, small teams, and large units must be able to adjust their equipment. They must understand the fundamentals of cross-leveling essential equipment to avoid excess gear. Understanding and practicing these simple, yet often overlooked, skills can make a unit lighter, faster, and more lethal in mountainous terrain. No amount of training can change the body's reaction to carrying excessive loads. Analyzing the situation and the level of risk are the keys to determining what is mission essential. Virtually all surface waters are microbiologically contaminated. There are three types of disease-causing microorganisms: protozoa, bacteria, and viruses. 4-77. Protozoa are the largest of waterborne bugs measuring in the 1-micron range. Giardia and cryptosporidium are the most infamous of the group. The infective cysts and oocysts of protozoa are extremely robust and can survive for months in a water source. They thrive in domestic and wild animals, as well as humans. Cryptosporidium oocysts are known for their resistance to chemical treatment. Most disinfectants are ineffective, and the few that require long dwell times to do the job. 4-78.

Most disinfectants are ineffective, and the few that require long dwell times to do the job. 4-78. Bacteria are an order of magnitude smaller than protozoa measuring in the 0.2-micron range. The most well-known bacteria are Escherichia coli (commonly referred to as E. coli); others include campylobacter, salmonella, and shigella. Bacteria are not as hearty, surviving in water for weeks instead of months. However, unlike protozoa and viruses, which require a host to multiply, some bacteria grow in water and are found in higher numbers than protozoa and viruses. Both animals and humans often carry bacteria, such as protozoa; as a result, many water sources are contaminated with bacteria. Beware of water sources near agricultural operations. 4-79. Viruses-some notorious waterborne viruses are poliovirus, hepatitis, and norovirus. Waterborne viruses are very resilient and can survive for months in water. Viruses are generally species-specific; in other words, those that infect animals do not infect humans and vice versa. Because of this and the modern sanitation measures taken in developed countries, not as many water sources are contaminated with viruses.

It is best to avoid water sources such as mining tailing ponds or those near agricultural operations. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 55

Chapter 4 WATER PURIFICATION 4-81. Water should always be treated. No matter how clean the snow or water may appear, it should always be considered contaminated. There are many techniques to purify water, each with inherent advantages and disadvantages. 4-82. Boiling kills biological contaminants but does not eliminate chemical contaminants. Filtration should also be used if chemical contaminants are suspected. To ensure all biological contaminants have been killed, let the water boil for 1 minute. This method requires time and fuel while allowing water to be treated away from the source. 4-83. Chemical treatment can be accomplished with iodine or chlorine dioxide. These treatments are available commercially and come with instructions for proper use. Chemical treatment will kill almost all biological contaminants but are ineffective against cryptosporidium. It requires time for these chemical treatments to be effective, and, in cold temperatures, it takes longer. This method allows water to be treated away from the source and on the go. 4-84. UV lights are an effective way to kill all biological contaminants but do not treat for chemical contaminants. They require batteries and in cloudy debris-filled water, it may not kill all contaminants. Ensure water is filtered if it is cloudy

UV lights are an effective way to kill all biological contaminants but do not treat for chemical contaminants. They require batteries and in cloudy debris-filled water, it may not kill all contaminants. Ensure water is filtered if it is cloudy before use. This method can be used away from the source. 4-85. Filters are compact and lightweight. They work by filtering out particulate, chemicals, and biological contaminants. Filters are not capable of removing any chemical contaminants that are dissolved in the water. Certain filters may not be able to filter out smaller biological contaminants as the pores of the filter are too large to remove them. These types of filters are designed to remove waterborne protozoa and bacteria but not viruses. The benefit of these types of filters is that water moves more rapidly through them. Filters that can filter smaller contaminants are often referred to as water purifiers. Water purifiers are designed to remove protozoa, bacteria, and viruses, offering a higher level of defense by combating all three. Such a lee is an attractive bivouac site from the standpoint of wind protection. 56 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment Note that such a lee area is often an area of maximum snow deposit. Frequent requirements to dig out vehicles, walkways, and weapons positions may offset the wind-free advantages of a lee site during snowfall or snow-blowing weather. Avalanche hazard areas must be avoided. Cold air is heavier than warm air and frequently settles in valleys. If tactically feasible, it is better to establish a bivouac up the hillside above the valley floor and below the timberline. BIVOUAC SITE LOCATION 4-90. The following are considerations for selecting a bivouac site in the mountains: * Cover and concealment-cover and concealment from air and ground observation is essential for the bivouac area. Chapter 5 Avalanche World War I is remembered for the brutal fighting in the trenches in France and Belgium. However, in the fighting between Italy and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Soldiers saw some of the most intense mountain fighting in human history. After the Italians checked the Austrian offensive through the passes of the Alps, both sides fought higher and higher into the mountains. Small, light units of mountaineers clashed over new ground high in the peaks, while the armies dug in on the peaks they had secured. Positions and paths were blasted out of the rock and carved through the glaciers to move personnel and materiel to the fighting in the heights. By the winter of 1916, the line had mostly stabilized, and both armies were hunkering down for winter. Both sides had established extensive networks of trails and camps to support their forward positions; however, much of the infrastructure had been built in avalanche paths. In the second week of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing massive avalanches across the range. Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim

of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing massive avalanches across the range. Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim picture. The lowest estimates place casualties at around 4,000 during the storm. Some records support numbers as high as 10,000. Today, their bodies are still melting out of the glaciers below. SECTION I - AVALANCHE HAZARDS 5-1. During winter months and throughout the year, snow covers the slopes. Steep, snow-covered terrain, in addition to mobility challenges and fall hazards, present the risk of avalanches. This hazard is easy to underestimate. It is not clearly visible, and, due to the complexity of the factors involved, there is a high degree of uncertainty, but the consequences of ignoring the hazard are high. Avalanches have taken the lives of more troops engaged in mountain warfare than all other terrain hazards combined. 5-2. An avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in the mountains during the winter, these instabilities

avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in the mountains during the winter, these instabilities in the snowpack may make large areas too dangerous for travel. These snow slopes may appear unthreatening but may have weak layers buried in the snowpack that can be easily triggered. Military elements may gravitate into avalanche terrain to avoid steeper technical terrain or enemy observation. Avalanches can generate incredible destructive force, destroying equipment, killing or burying Soldiers, and blocking key roads. Whether operating dismounted in high alpine terrain or as a mounted force in valley bottoms, units must be aware of avalanche hazards. They must incorporate the evaluation of avalanche danger into the planning process and learn to recognize and avoid hazardous terrain. (See figure 5-1, page 64.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 63

Chapter 5 Figure 5-1. Movement through avalanche terrain AVALANCHE ELEMENTS 5-3. Avalanches occur when the weight of accumulated snow on a slope exceeds the cohesive forces that hold the snow in place. There are three elements needed to create an avalanche: an unstable snowpack, terrain steep enough to slide, and a trigger that initiates the failure of bonds holding the snow in place. SNOWPACK 5-4. Layers of snow accumulate with each new snow or wind event. Variation in temperature and atmospheric conditions form layers with different types of snow crystals. These layers are subject to changes in texture and strength throughout the winter, as they are exposed to sun, wind, and temperature changes. Each layer in the snowpack will have distinct characteristics. Strong layers are made up of well-bonded, small, rounded grains. Weak layers are made up of larger, angular, poorly bonded grains. Snowpack Concerns 5-5. Instabilities are weaknesses within the snowpack as described below (see figure 5-2): * Weak layers-weak layers may collapse under load, initiating an avalanche. Poorly bonded crystals can act like ball bearings between stronger layers. Weak layers can change over time, becoming stronger, denser layers. This happens more quickly in temperatures above freezing. However, many

layers-weak layers may collapse under load, initiating an avalanche. Poorly bonded crystals can act like ball bearings between stronger layers. Weak layers can change over time, becoming stronger, denser layers. This happens more quickly in temperatures above freezing. However, many avalanche cycles are due to weak layers that resist this change and retain their large grain size and 64 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Avalanche * * angular shape for long periods. These types of layers are known as "persistent" weak layers. These are common in prolonged colder temperatures. Weak bonds between layers-differences in the size and compositions of crystals between layers inhibit bonding. Large differences between layers are the primary source of instability. Bed surface-the bed surface is the surface over which a fracture and subsequent avalanche release occurs. Smooth, uniform sliding surfaces provide less friction to hold the snow in place. Examples are firm old snow layers, rain crusts, and sun crusts. Figure 5-2. Snowpack layers Loading 5-6. When instability exists in the snowpack, another important factor is the load placed on top of the weak layer. With the added weight of accumulated snow, it increases the shear forces within the snowpack: * New snow-during snowstorms, snowfall will rapidly increase the forces placed on the snowpack. Snowfall of more than 2.5 centimeters (cm) (1 inch) of snow an hour or more than 30 cm (1 foot) of snow in 24 hours is considered critical loading. Avoid traveling in avalanche terrain during critical loading. * Wind loading-sustained winds will transport snow from windward slopes and ridge tops, depositing it in sheltered features on

30 cm (1 foot) of snow in 24 hours is considered critical loading. Avoid traveling in avalanche terrain during critical loading. * Wind loading-sustained winds will transport snow from windward slopes and ridge tops, depositing it in sheltered features on leeward aspects. With high winds, even small deposits of new snow can produce significant loading. Top loading occurs when wind deposits snow over the top of a ridge. Side loading (or cross loading) occurs when snow is blown across the slope and deposited in gullies or on the leeward sides of ridges. * Rain-rain rapidly increases the load on the snowpack and erodes bonds between snow crystals and layers. After a period of sustained cold where weak layers have been preserved in the snowpack, rain can produce dense, wet avalanches that are very destructive. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 65

Chapter 5 TERRAIN FACTORS 5-7. Terrain is the second factor that determines if an avalanche can occur. The character of a snowpack and opportunities for whether instabilities develop are determined by its elevation and aspect. A slope's characteristics-slope angle, shape, and physical characteristics-determine the likelihood of a slide. Recognizing and avoiding avalanche terrain are the keys to managing avalanche risk. Elevation 5-8. Precipitation, temperature, and wind often vary significantly at different elevations. This results in differences in the snowpack, all of which influence the type, size, distribution, and sensitivity of avalanches. 5-9. Increased precipitation-as weather systems are lifted over mountains (orthographic lift), the air cools and can hold less moisture, causing additional precipitation at elevation. Increased precipitation causes increased loads on the snowpack. 5-10. Temperature-warming in the snowpack temporarily increases instability as bonds melt but improves stability when it re-freezes. Cooler temperatures at higher elevations inhibit stabilization. Instabilities can persist for much longer. Aspect to Wind 5-11. Sustained winds of 15 mph or higher transport snow from the windward aspect of the slope and deposit it in the form of wind slabs on the leeward slopes. Leeward slopes can accumulate three to five times the amount of snow that falls

15 mph or higher transport snow from the windward aspect of the slope and deposit it in the form of wind slabs on the leeward slopes. Leeward slopes can accumulate three to five times the amount of snow that falls in sheltered locations. Slopes on the windward side have much of their new snow "scoured" off by the wind and are generally more stable than leeward slopes. Leeward slopes tend to form dangerous cornices and large, unstable slabs of snow. Aspect to Sun 5-12. Solar radiation causes drastic temperature swings in the snowpack. South-facing slopes can be dangerous on warm, sunny days immediately following storms. However, over time, these slopes stabilize as the added heat promotes bonding between layers. Snow on north-facing slopes does not stabilize as quickly and is more hazardous through most of the winter. Note. This effect is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere. Start Zone Characteristics 5-13. The shape of the slope will also affect the forces within the snowpack, concentrating tension in specific areas where it requires less force to trigger an avalanche. For this reason, anchors can be starting points for initial failure to occur, and fractures often run from tree to tree or rock to rock. Figure 5-4. Slope shape Terrain Traps 5-15. Terrain traps are features that increase the consequences of being caught in an avalanche. Examples include cliffs, gullies, creeks, lakes, trees, benches, or roads where debris will pile up, crevasses, or bergschrunds. Some terrain traps increase trauma during an avalanche. Others increase burial depth, making survival more unlikely. TRIGGERS 5-16. All avalanche triggers, whether caused by natural forces or human actions, are due to overloading the cohesive strength of the snowpack: * Natural-avalanches may be triggered by new snow, falling rock, snow, ice, or smaller avalanches. Solar warming erodes bonds and can trigger avalanches. Naturally occurring avalanches are a critical warning sign that the conditions for an avalanche exist on similar slopes. If natural avalanches are possible, human triggered avalanches are likely. * Human-most victims trigger the avalanches that kill them. People apply significant force to the snowpack.
