If natural avalanches are possible, human triggered avalanches are likely. * Human-most victims trigger the avalanches that kill them. People apply significant force to the snowpack. The impact of that force depends on snow density and distribution of force. A Soldier traveling on skis will not stress the snowpack as deep as a Soldier on foot will. Vehicles apply even more force. When a collapse occurs in a weak layer, it can propagate long distances up or across the slope. TYPES OF AVALANCHES 5-17. Avalanches can be categorized into two broad categories: loose snow and slab avalanches. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) Loose snow slides start with less snow and pick up more snow as they descend. Slab avalanches occur when one or more layers of cohesive snow break away as a unit and are generally more destructive. 68 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Avalanche 5-18. There are many variations of these types, each with distinct characteristics. These characteristics are defined by the structures within the snowpack, how an avalanche is released, and where it is found in the terrain. These avalanche problems guide group discussions, route planning, terrain choices, and the observations made during snowpack evaluation. LOOSE-DRY AVALANCHES 5-19. A loose-dry avalanche is a release of dry, unconsolidated snow. These avalanches occur within layers of soft snow near the surface of the snowpack. Loose-dry avalanches start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. Other names for loose-dry avalanches include point-release avalanches or sluffs. Loose-dry avalanches can trigger slab avalanches that break into deeper snow layers. Loose-dry avalanches are usually less dangerous than other avalanche problems but can be hazardous when combined with terrain traps, such as gullies, rocks, dense timber, cliffs, or crevasses. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) STORM SLAB AVALANCHES 5-20. A storm slab avalanche is a release of a soft cohesive layer (a slab) of new snow that breaks within the storm snow or on the old snow surface. Storm-slab problems last between a few hours and a few days but often stabilize quickly.

Storm-slab problems last between a few hours and a few days but often stabilize quickly. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) WIND SLAB AVALANCHES 5-21. A wind slab avalanche is the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) formed by the wind. Wind transports snow from the upwind sides of terrain features and deposits snow on the downwind side. Wind slabs are often smooth and rounded, sound hollow sometimes, and can range from soft to hard. Wind slabs form in specific areas and are confined to lee and cross-loaded terrain features. They can be avoided by sticking to sheltered or wind-scoured areas. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) PERSISTENT SLAB AVALANCHES 5-22. A persistent slab avalanche is a release of a cohesive layer of soft to hard snow (a slab) in the middle to upper snowpack, when the bond to an underlying persistent weak layer breaks. Persistent weak layers can continue to produce avalanches for days, weeks, or even months, making them challenging to manage. As additional snow and wind events build a thicker slab

snowpack, when the bond to an underlying persistent weak layer breaks. Persistent weak layers can continue to produce avalanches for days, weeks, or even months, making them challenging to manage. As additional snow and wind events build a thicker slab on top of the persistent weak layer, this avalanche problem may develop into a deep, persistent slab. They can be triggered by light loads and last weeks after the last storm. The slabs often propagate in surprising and unpredictable ways, making this problem difficult to predict and manage, and require a wide safety buffer to handle the uncertainty. The best ways to manage the risk from persistent slabs are to make conservative terrain choices. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) Note. Storm slabs and wind slabs formed over persistent weak layers are also considered persistent slabs. DEEP, PERSISTENT SLAB AVALANCHES 5-23. A deep, persistent slab avalanche is a release of a thick, cohesive layer of hard snow (a slab), when the bond breaks between the slab and an underlying "persistent" weak layer, deep in the snowpack or near the ground. Deep, persistent slabs are difficult to trigger but are very destructive and dangerous because of the large mass of snow involved.

These avalanches occur within layers of wet snow near the surface of the snowpack but may quickly gouge into lower snowpack layers. Like dry-loose avalanches, they start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. They often carve channels or paths through the snowpack to which subsequent avalanches are constrained. They move slowly but can contain enough mass to cause significant damage to trees, cars, or buildings. To avoid wet-loose avalanches, travel when the snow surface is colder and stronger. Avalanche SECTION III - AVALANCHE SEARCH AND RESCUE 5-40. The primary risk mitigation tool in avalanche terrain is avoidance. In the planning phase, Soldiers should make every effort to patrol routes that avoid avalanche hazards. The planning phase includes having clear decision points from which to evaluate conditions and viable alternate routes. However, when evaluating an avalanche hazard, there is often a high degree of uncertainty. When mistakes are made, the consequences are high. Avalanches produce incredible energy. Soldiers caught in an avalanche may be injured or killed by blunt force trauma from collisions with rock, ice, and trees. If they come to rest with an intact air pocket, they may succumb to hypothermia or shock. However, most avalanche victims die from asphyxiation. Without an air pocket, unconsciousness may come in minutes, followed rapidly by permeant brain injury and death. Evidence has shown that after 15 minutes, the chances of surviving complete burial decreases from 90 percent to 30 percent. A probe line is a systematic search, online, through the entire debris field. It is a slow process and requires many rescuers. Chapter 6 Mountain Mobility A unit's ability to maneuver through difficult and hazardous terrain provides it with access to the most tactically advantageous areas in the mountains. Units with Soldiers trained to a high level of mobility can move further, faster, and more safely through all levels of terrain. Mobility skill is the primary tool to manage risk when there is a fall hazard. Rope systems and belays can be used to mitigate fall risk during movement but require more time to complete, more technical training to accomplish, and can result in increased exposure to enemy attack. By far, the greatest combat multiplier in the mountains is high mobility skill. Units anticipating combat operations should focus on building individual movement skills over nearly all other special technical or tactical skills. SECTION I - INDIVIDUAL MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES 6-1. The speed at which the unit can move, the complexity of terrain they can negotiate unroped, and the violence of action they can muster as a team on the objective are all determined by the mobility of the unit's weakest members. Properly equipped units with mobility skills are more likely to outmaneuver the enemy in physically demanding and hazardous terrain. Soldiers who have

muster as a team on the objective are all determined by the mobility of the unit's weakest members. Properly equipped units with mobility skills are more likely to outmaneuver the enemy in physically demanding and hazardous terrain. Soldiers who have been trained in mobility techniques can take advantage of terrain above operational level 2. This provides commanders with access to the highest and most difficult to reach points of domination in their areas of operation. For those untrained in mountaineering, such terrain can prove too hazardous to move in. However, units well-trained to maneuver here can take advantage of reduced combat risks during all types of combat operations by owning ground that most enemy forces cannot access, granting them overwhelming tactical advantage. As a result, individual mobility skills training should always be a high priority for units anticipating these operations. MOBILITY 6-2. Individual mobility comprises many factors, the most important of which are fitness and movement techniques. Soldiers can increase their mobility by practicing the movement techniques specific to negotiating rough terrain. The hallmarks of mobility are balance, surefootedness, and net endurance. The results are reduced likelihood of slipping or falling, reduced energy expended, increased speed, and the ability to focus on other critical tasks. Grassy slopes are usually composed of small tussocks of growth rather than one continuous field. When ascending, step on the upper side of each hummock or tussock, where the ground is more level. Mountain Mobility 6-24. General techniques for ascending: * As terrain becomes steeper, routes should adopt a traversing or switchback pattern. This involves moving diagonally up and across a slope, then turning back and doing the same in the opposite direction as necessary. This switchback pattern reduces the intensity and demand on large muscle groups, slows the onset of fatigue, and allows Soldiers to maintain situational awareness. Charging in a straight line up a steep hill is more demanding, results in more extreme fatigue and longer recovery time, and increases the likelihood of slips, falls, and injury. This technique should be avoided unless speed is critical, and all members of the group are highly fit and experienced moving this way. * The rest step technique involves locking out the rear leg briefly with each step. This gives muscles a micro rest with each step and results in greater endurance over long movements. (See figure 6-2, page 88.) * Pressure breathing-this technique involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the lungs of air. This does two positive things. First, it ensures all carbon dioxide is pushed out of the lungs, reducing the likelihood of cramping, and making more

involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the lungs of air. This does two positive things. First, it ensures all carbon dioxide is pushed out of the lungs, reducing the likelihood of cramping, and making more space for oxygenated air. Second, the negative pressure created in the lungs makes it easier to pull lower pressure air into them when moving at higher altitudes. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 87

or smaller, that are common in the mountains and are a challenge to ascend. The experience is like climbing sand, except that the loose rock can be rough on ankles and lower legs. Climbers should avoid ascending scree fields, if possible, as they demand the expenditure of much more energy than other surfaces. Soldiers should kick in with the toe of the upper foot so that a step is formed in the loose scree. After determining that the step is stable, the Soldier transfers weight to the upper leg, then steps up, and repeats the process with the lower foot. Chapter 6 SCRAMBLING 6-33. Scrambling is the act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking techniques but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques. It is perhaps the most dangerous means of mobility in which snow and ice are not present. At the lowest level, scrambling involves simply placing a hand or hands on features periodically to help maintain balance and improve efficiency during movement. At the higher level, scrambling involves Soldiers making multiple easy rock-climbing moves, followed by several steps walking, and repeating that sequence throughout an ascent. 6-34. Typically, 3rd-class terrain is where Soldiers begin scrambling, but just exactly what terrain and terrain features require is determined largely by the mobility skill of the individual Soldier. Soldiers with low-mobility skill will need to use hands more often, especially if a fall risk is present, which will slow their movement. Soldiers with higher mobility skills need to use their hands less often for balance enabling them to move faster even when a fall risk is present. 6-35. Types of Contact 6-56. Though counterintuitive, often pushing rather than pulling is required during climbing. Using downward pressure involves pushing down on a feature with the hands to allow unweighting of the other hand or one foot for movement to the next hold. Using counterpressure involves pushing away from features to allow a hand or foot to be unweighted for movement. (See figure 6-5, page 94.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 93

Chapter 6 Figure 6-5. Downward or counterpressure 6-57. Occasionally, the holds available put the climber out of balance, but repositioning the body (usually by extending a leg to the left or right) improves the climber's balance. This technique is called counterbalancing and often allows the climber greater reach. (See figure 6-6.) Often the climber can find a microfeature to touch or apply slight pressure to with the foot improving the security of the move. 94 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-6. Counterbalance 6-58. Occasionally, the climber must switch hands or feet on a hold to make the next move. Sometimes the hold can be shared temporarily by two hands or feet, even if they are unsecure, while the lead hand or lead foot moves. Other times, the second hand or foot may need to use a temporary, perhaps less desirable hold, while the lead one moves. 6-59. Dynamic moves are sudden, explosive moves where climbers throw themselves out of balance, potentially even losing contact with the rock, to reach another hold. These moves must be calculated carefully because failing to execute them perfectly usually results in a fall. Slab and Face Climbing 6-60. Slabs are typically smoother, lower angle rock features. They can be large or small. Comparatively, they provide the climber with few hands and footholds and require good footwork and balancing to climb. The primary technique used to climb them is smearing with the feet. This involves placing the sole of the boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The

This involves placing the sole of the boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The closer climbers can get to pushing perpendicular to the rock, the more friction they will create. (See figure 6-7, page 96.) Hands are usually used to help balance by pushing against the rock. Any microfeature that can be found will improve the security of climbing slabby terrain. Climbing slabby rock helps build confidence in footwork and good balance skills. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 95

Chapter 6 6-61. Face climbing is what is commonly associated with rock climbing. Face climbs are typically suitably featured rock faces (cliffs) where climbers employ a wide variety of basic moves to ascending. Climbers spend most of their time facing the rock, like climbing a ladder. Many footholds are small or sloped and require edging or smearing to be effective; others are larger. (See figure 6-8.) Many techniques for using handholds exist. (See figure 6-8.) Using knees should be avoided because they are more likely to slip than good footwear. 6-62. Most slab or face climbing terrain appropriate to military operations can be climbed in combat boots, mountaineering boots, or approach shoes. Moderate to difficult climbs require climbing shoes. (See figure 6-9.) Figure 6-7. Footholds Figure 6-8. Handhold techniques 96 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-9. Slab body position Resting During Climbing 6-63. Resting is critical during sustained rock climbing. Any opportunity to stand up and let go or lightly hold on with the hands should be taken. Sometimes the body or a body part can be wedged into a large crack, allowing the climber to relax. Often, the only rests available are between moves while looking for the next hold. When not actively moving, climbers should keep their weight on their skeletal system as much as possible. This means locking out legs or arms and providing muscles with a brief rest. Doing this is particularly important to preserve arm strength. Often one arm and the climbers' feet can support their weight while they shake out the other arm and hand. (See figure 6-10, page 98.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 97

Chapter 6 Figure 6-10. Rest or shake out Specific Moves 6-64. Mantling involves pulling down with both arms on the edge of a ledge type feature until the chest is ledge height, then transitioning to pushing down on the ledge while walking the feet up the face below. This move is common to climbing out of a swimming pool. (See figure 6-11.) 98 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility 6-65. Stemming involves placing the feet on features to the left and right of the body so that force is applied outward as well as down. Stemming is typically very stable and requires a relatively low amount of energy to maintain. (See figure 6-12, page 100.) 6-66. Underclinging involves gripping an overhanging rock feature with the hands, palm up, and pushing against a lower rock face with the feet. Underclings can be very stable but can be quite strenuous and tiring. Occasionally, underlings are the only means of getting through a section of climbing. (See figure 6-13, page 101.) 6-67. Liebacking involves using counterforce by pulling hard on a vertical or diagonal feature (such as a large flake) while pushing hard against the face of the rock. These moves are very strenuous because little or none of the climbers' weights is supported by their feet. In fact, leg muscles are being used to push away from the rock, so they are very taxing to the upper body. The climber's hands are then walked up the feature while the feet are walked up the face. Footholds on the face, however small, can be used to make liebacking easier and

so they are very taxing to the upper body. The climber's hands are then walked up the feature while the feet are walked up the face. Footholds on the face, however small, can be used to make liebacking easier and more secure. (See figure 6-14, page 102.) Figure 6-11. Mantling 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 99

Chapter 6 Figure 6-14. Liebacking Crack Climbing 6-68. Crack climbing requires a specific set of nonintuitive techniques that take quite a bit of practice to build proficiency in. While some climbs involving cracks can be climbed with weak or no crack technique, more difficult crack climbs require climbing shoes and good technique to be climbable. Mixed crack climbing involves using features on the rock face for footholds while using a prominent crack for handholds. (See figure 6-15.) Classic crack climbing involves moving up a prominent crack by alternately jamming hands or fingers and feet or toes and walking them up the crack. Often, one foot is placed out of the crack to the side for balance, even on a featureless face. Off-width crack climbing is the term for climbing cracks that are larger than fist and foot sized but not large enough to fit the entire body. These climbs are difficult. 102 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-15. Mixed face and crack climbing Jamming 6-69. A critical technique in climbing cracks involves placing a hand or foot into a crack and turning, twisting, or otherwise manipulating them so that they become temporarily jammed in the crack. A good jam can be achieved in a variety of ways depending on crack size, whether it has constrictions in it or not, and its position in relation to other holds on the climb. Jams can provide solid hands or footholds but are often uncomfortable or even painful. Crack size determines which jam technique to use for a given hold. Constrictions in the crack make jam holds more secure. Types of Hand Jams 6-70. Hand-sized jams are the easiest to perform. The hand is inserted open into the crack and then the fingers bent exert pressure against the walls of the crack. Often turning one hand thumb down is useful. Typically, leaning to the same side adds security to a thumb up hand jam. (See figure 6-16, page 104 for variations of hand jamming.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 103

Chapter 6 6-71. Fist jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are larger than those that work for hand jams. The same jamming principles apply, but climbers just insert their entire fist into the crack. (See figure 6-17 for variations of fist jamming.) 6-72. Finger jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are smaller than those that will accept a hand. The same jamming principles apply, but the climber only inserts their fingers, or parts of their fingers into the crack. Finger jamming is more difficult and can be painful for the joints. It is important to strengthen finger muscles prior to attempting to support substantial weight with finger jams to prevent joint strain. (See figure 6-18.) Types of Foot Jams 6-73. Foot jams involve turning the foot so that it fits into the crack and then twisting it so that the width of the foot wedges into the crack. This can be uncomfortable but can provide very secure footholds. (See figure 6-19.) 6-74. Toe jams are used in the same manner as foot jams, but in smaller cracks. (See figure 6-20, page 106.) Arm bars is a technique used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack and bending at the elbow to create a jam. (See figure 6-21, page 106.) 6-76. Chicken wing is a technique also used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack bent at the elbow and pushing against one wall of the crack with the hand to create a jam. Chapter 6 Figure 6-20. Toe jams Figure 6-21. Arm bar and chicken wing Dihedral and Chimney Climbing 6-77. Climbing dihedrals and chimneys involves positioning the body inside a feature and using counterpressure or stemming to make upward movement. These features can often make for less strenuous climbing due to the counterpressure positions allowing for more rests. A dihedral is two rock faces that meet to form a corner, like an open book. Often there is a crack where the two faces meet. Chimneys are roughly parallel-sided features. They could be like a vertical shaft or crack large enough to accept a whole body. 6-78. Dihedrals can usually be climbed with a combination of stemming and either crack or face climbing. Dihedrals are easier and less strenuous to climb when the two faces have multiple and large features. 6-79. Chimneys are often unpleasant features to climb but provide a lot of security during movement. The basic technique for climbers is to position their body in the chimney and use counterpressure by pushing with arms, legs, and back against opposing sides. (See figures 6-22 through 6-24, pages 107 through 109, for variations in chimney climbing techniques.) Often during chimney climbing, it is

position their body in the chimney and use counterpressure by pushing with arms, legs, and back against opposing sides. Often during chimney climbing, it is necessary to attach climbing packs to the harness hanging below the climber. 106 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-24. Chimney climbing technique Traversing 6-80. Traversing is moving laterally on the rock. This is often necessary because the features that make up a rock route are not always continuous or travel straight up a face. Traversing often involves a series of placement exchanges. Most traversing is done facing the rock. 6-81. Hand traversing requires a ledge, flake, other horizontal feature, or a series of horizontally oriented large handholds. Climbers' hands walk their way across the features while their feet walk their way across a face below. (See figure 6-25, page 110.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 109

Chapter 6 6-82. Steep traverse is a technique often used when handholds are not as good, but decent footholds are present. Climbers lean heavily in the direction they want to move and place hands on available holds, and then walk their feet in the same direction using available footholds. Sometimes a crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26.) Figure 6-25. Hand traverse Topping Out or Gaining Ledges 6-83. Topping out or gaining a ledge can be one of the more challenging parts of climbing. Often low holds located near where climbers want to put their feet need to be used to get over the edge. Often, a mantling technique is effective. Most importantly, climbers should avoid laying on their belly on the edge when moving because it may be difficult to get their feel back on the rock, and they may slide off on sloped ledges. A crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26 for the proper technique.) 110 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-26. Gaining ledges Down Climbing 6-84. Down climbing is far more difficult than climbing up and takes much practice to gain proficiency. This is largely because rock features are often difficult to identify from above. They are easily obscured by other features above them or even the climber's body parts. However, down climbing is an important skill to practice, as it is often necessary to do in 3rd- and 4th-class terrain. 6-85. Facing out is a technique used on low angle rock. Climbers face out and use their hands for stability behind and below their body while moving their feet down to the next hold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-86. Walking down a slab is a technique that involves simply walking down slabby rock while maintaining maximum friction and balance. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-87. Facing sideways involves climbers facing to the side and side stepping down to lower footholds while controlling and balancing their movement using handholds above. Climbers use this technique on steeper rock. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-88. Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the rock. Climbers lower themselves

movement using handholds above. Climbers use this technique on steeper rock. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-88. Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the rock. Climbers lower themselves down with their arms, keeping their body away from the rock so they can see footholds below, and then transition their weight onto the next foothold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 111

Chapter 6 Figure 6-27. Down climbing TRAINING FOR ROCK CLIMBING 6-89. Beginner rock-climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope belay techniques (see chapter 10). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of rock climbing is relatively low risk and has a high payoff for developing mobility skills. One restriction is that sites do not often allow large groups to be actively engaged. Thus, climbing training should be planned along with concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging to climbers but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to build skills. A motivational rather than critical atmosphere is most effective when building climbing skills. 6-90. Climbing training for more advanced military mountaineers can be conducted the same way, just on more challenging routes, but should also be conducted in a multipitch setting that more accurately reproduces conditions of climbing during military operations. This setting requires the development of lead climbing and route-finding skills, which are critical to the advanced military mountaineer. 6-91. Leaders should try to learn the etiquette associated with climbing before using civilian climbing areas. 112 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility SECTION II - MOVEMENT OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-92. Deep snow, steep powdery slopes, glare ice, and frozen waterfalls all present significant challenges to movement. The basic individual movement principles and skill development necessary for movement under other surface conditions also apply to movement over snow and ice. However, additional skills are necessary for efficiency and safety. Specialized equipment is required in even the easiest snow or ice-covered terrain. MOBILITY OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-93. Fitness and movement techniques are the foundation of moving through snow or up steep ice. However, identifying and selecting secure foot placements can be difficult because traction is drastically reduced. Movement without specialized equipment, such as crampons or skis, is difficult under almost all conditions above 1st-class terrain. Even when it is possible, deep snow requires a substantial amount of energy to move through unaided. Anything deeper than calf-deep snow will impede movement in even easy terrain, and a few inches of snow or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills

or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills can only be developed through experience and repetition. Units that train their Soldiers to proficiency in these conditions can move faster, safer, and access terrain that others cannot. EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE 6-94. Skis provide substantial floatation in deep snow and require the least amount of energy for movement. This is especially true for downhill movement where much energy can be saved over walking. There are varieties of ski systems available for movement over snow, but those most suited to military mountaineering are called alpine touring skis. The ski itself is like a downhill ski, but the binding allows the heel to release for movement over flat or uphill terrain. It can also be locked down for greater control when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is

when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is necessary for use with skis. In the steepest terrain, a dedicated rigid plastic ski boot may be required. Compatibility between boots and bindings must be considered. (See figure 6-28, page 114.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 113

Chapter 6 Figure 6-28. Alpine touring skis 6-95. Snowshoes are another tool available to Soldiers for moving over deep snow. Modern snowshoes provide sufficient floatation and traction for moving through snow on fairly steep (class 2) slopes and should be small and light enough to pack, if necessary. Snowshoes work with any boot. (See figure 6-29.) 114 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-29. Snowshoes 6-96. Ski poles are typically used with snowshoes and skis to provide more lateral stability and balance. Ski poles can be used to provide excellent support for weapons systems during firing from the prone, kneeling, and standing positions. 6-97. Sleds are useful for carrying large amounts of equipment, such as bivouac equipment, heavy weapons, food and water, or other supplies. They range in size, shape, and weight, all of which should be considered before selection for military operations. Four- and ten-Soldier Ahkio-style sleds are available through the military supply system. These are designed to carry all group sustainment equipment (for example, tents, stoves, fuel) for a four- or ten-Soldier group. These come with a cover and rigid poles, convenient for dragging up and downhill. (See figure 6-30, page 116.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 115

Chapter 6 Figure 6-30. Ahkio sleds 6-98. Crampons attach to the Soldier's boot to provide traction on ice and snow. There are two basic types: general mountaineering crampons and ice climbing crampons. Mountaineering crampons have less aggressive points. They are designed for use in steep snow and on low-angle ice and can be used for ice climbing but are not ideal. Ice climbing crampons have points that are more aggressive and are typically more rigid. They are designed for steep ice climbing but can be used in snow and low angle ice as well. Crampons work best when paired with a stiff leather or rigid plastic mountaineering boot. They do not work well with issued cold-weather combat boots. (See figure 6-31.) Figure 6-31. Crampons 6-99. Mountain axes are important tools for movement over steep snow and occasional low-angle ice. The two types of axes usually used in alpine terrain are general mountain axes and hybrid mountain axes. General axes are designed for steep snow and hybrid axes are designed for steep snow and low-angle ice climbing. Ice axes have an adze to the rear of the pick for chopping snow and ice. (See figure 6-32.) 116 TC 3-97.61 26 November

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-32. Mountain axes 6-100. Ice tools are modified ice axes designed for steep ice climbing. They are much more aggressive and curved to help obtain solid sticks in hard vertical ice and over bulges. They are less effective in snow than general or hybrid axes because of their short length. Ice tools can include an adze or a hammerhead. Hammers are used for placing pitons during mixed climbing. (See figure 6-33, page 118.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 117

Chapter 6 Figure 6-33. Ice tools MILITARY OPERATIONS IN SNOW- AND ICE-COVERED TERRAIN 6-101. Snow and ice present many additional challenges for units that need to move in mountainous terrain. Specialized equipment, training, and experience are necessary to move in it safely and effectively. Whether the challenges are deep snow, slick slopes, or steep sections of vertical ice, they will prove substantial obstacles for unprepared units. Units anticipating operating in such terrain and conditions should train in them prior to engaging in combat operations. 6-102. Even with proper equipment and training, it is unlikely that larger units can move in terrain steeper than 2nd-class terrain without ropes due to the high risk of long sliding falls. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be trained to move over ice and snow and tasked with finding routes and establishing rope systems for larger units. (See chapter 11 for establishing fixed-rope systems for troop movement in steep terrain and ATP 3-21.50 for crossing VDA TTP.) 118 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility MOVEMENT OVER SNOW 6-103. Low- to moderate-angle snow slopes found on or adjacent to valleys are primary avenues of movement for military units operating in winter conditions. Steeper slopes in gullies and passes are often the easiest routes through even steeper rocky features around them. Though challenging to move over, these often provide the best access to points of domination in alpine terrain. 6-104. Techniques for moving over snowy surfaces change IAW slope and surface conditions. Some soft snow increases physical strain but can increase the security of foot placements. During movement, breaks should be taken more frequently and for shorter durations in cold weather to assist with moisture management. This helps prevent overheating, which can cause problems once movements stop. Snow deeper than calf-height makes movement difficult without skis or snowshoes. Hard-packed snow slopes requiring special techniques and equipment or falls that could result in serious injury or death are likely. 6-105. A thorough analysis of avalanche threat should be conducted prior to moving over slopes that could be exposed to avalanche risk. Terrain at any risk for avalanche should be avoided. All Soldiers moving in potential avalanche terrain must be equipped with avalanche protective equipment and

threat should be conducted prior to moving over slopes that could be exposed to avalanche risk. Terrain at any risk for avalanche should be avoided. (See chapter 5 for more information on avalanche considerations.) BOOT PACKING 6-106. The boot-packing method requires the least amount of training and special equipment. The same techniques can be used in mountain walking; however, there is often less traction. During the boot-packing method, Soldiers move slower and minor slips and falls should be expected. In deeper soft snow, Soldiers should step in the tracks left by the Soldier in front of them. This packs them into hard steps and makes movement less difficult. Rotate lead Soldiers to prevent fatigue. 6-107. Crampons are strongly recommended for moving on hard-packed slopes. However, if crampons are not available, there are a few techniques to use to improve the security of foot placements. Step kicking involves kicking the toe or edge of the boot into the surface with each step creating a small depression, which improves traction. Mountain axes can be used as a

to use to improve the security of foot placements. Step kicking involves kicking the toe or edge of the boot into the surface with each step creating a small depression, which improves traction. Mountain axes can be used as a third point of contact, allowing the body to gain more traction. The axe is typically held by its head in the uphill hand, with the pick to the rear (cane position). Steps can be cut into the slope using the axe's adze to improve foot placement security. (See figure 6-34, page 120.) This technique is effective for short distances but is very time-consuming. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 119

Chapter 6 Figure 6-34. Step cutting GLISSADING 6-108. Glissading is a technique used to descend low to moderate angle slopes by sliding in the seated position and using a mountain axe as a brake. (See figure 6-35.) Glissading allows Soldiers to descend appropriate slopes very quickly and efficiently, thereby saving significant time and energy. Specific conditions are required for glissading to be appropriate. The slope should not have any obstacles (such as trees, rocks, drop offs, crevasses) in the slide path, and it should have sufficient soft snow on the surface to allow Soldiers to control the speed of the slide. Glissading should never be done on hard-packed snow or ice surfaces. Crampons should be removed prior to glissading to ensure injuries to lower extremities are not caused by a crampon becoming caught on something during the slide. 6-109. Glissading is conducted by sitting in the snow and positioning the midpoint of a mountain axe shaft against one hip with the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain

the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain axe pick should always face forward (away from the Soldier) to prevent injury. Soldiers then initiate the slide on their buttocks using the axe spike as a brake. To slow down, Soldiers rotate the spike downward, pressing it deeper into the snowpack and increasing friction. To speed up, Soldiers rotate the spike away from the snowpack, decreasing friction. Adequate time should be allowed between Soldiers sliding in the same glissade path to ensure a collision does not occur should a Soldier stop shortly mid-slide. 120 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-35. Glissading FLATFOOTING 6-110. Flatfooting is the term for numerous techniques that increase security and efficiency of movement over snow and ice slopes. These techniques involve the use of both crampons and a mountain axe. The key principle of flatfooting is to position the body so that all crampon points are embedded in the snow surface. This provides maximum security for foot placements. These techniques are particularly critical to safe movement over steep, hard-packed snow. Flatfooting with heavy loads requires greater proficiency. Flatfooting techniques are much more difficult to perform in flexible boots or with loose sloppy crampons. (See figure 6-36, page 122.) 6-111. Crampons substantially increase the security of foot placements when used properly. However, walking in them forces the Soldier's gait to change and can take some practice getting used to. They must be sized properly and snugged tight to the boot, so Soldiers' boots do not slide around in the crampon introducing instability to their foot placements. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 121

Chapter 6 Figure 6-36. Flatfooting Ascending 6-112. Lower-angle slopes can be ascended using a diagonal traverse or switchback technique. More security can be gained from pointing the toe downhill some when placing the foot. Mountain axes or an ice tool can also be used in cane position the same way previously mentioned. (See figure 6-37.) 6-113. As terrain gets steeper, maximizing crampon point contact with the surface becomes more difficult. Footwork techniques used in rock climbing, such as edging, are very insecure when wearing crampons. They should not be used. Ankles must be rolled somewhat downhill to ensure crampon points are embedded in the surface. Turning the downhill foot so that the toe points downhill increases security by making it easier to engage the crampon points on the outside edge of the foot. Figure 6-37. Ice axe uses in low-angle terrain 122 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility 6-114. To obtain secure foot placements, lean the body away from the slope to increase pressure on crampon points. This becomes more important as surface conditions get firmer. Generally, it is easier to stay in balance and achieve solid foot placements by taking smaller steps. Moving diagonally up slope makes this easier to execute. 6-115. Flatfooting, using a mountain axe in a cross-body position. To perform this technique, the Soldier stands sideways to the slope. The mountain axe head is held in the downhill hand and the shaft held low in the uphill hand. The uphill foot is placed perpendicular to the slope and the downhill foot is placed similarly, but with the toe pointed downhill as much as comfort demands. The axe spike is then forced into the snowpack uphill from the feet far enough so that most of the Soldier's weight is transitioned onto it. This provides balance and security during foot movement. The downhill foot is moved across and placed above the uphill foot. If the crossover step is too awkward, it can be moved to a position just below the uphill foot, but this method is less efficient. The Soldier's weight is then transitioned onto the newly placed foot so that the uphill foot may be moved upslope. The process is then repeated, starting with replacing the axe uphill and the Soldier moves in a generally diagonal path up the slope. (See figure 6-38.) Figure 6-38. Chapter 6 6-117. Front pointing involves kicking into the slope with the toe of the boot so that all front crampon points become embedded in the surface. The Soldier leans forward slightly locking the ankle so that the sole of the foot is held perpendicular to the slope. If the heel is too low or too high, or only the large front points are embedded, then the foot placement will be less secure and may fail. The Soldier stands up on the placement using hands or mountain axe for balance and repeats kicking in with the other foot higher on the slope. This process is repeated as the Soldier generally moves straight up the slope. The front-pointing technique is very effective and allows for faster movement in steep terrain but is more physically taxing. The Soldier's calf muscles become fatigued quickly using this technique. The front-pointing technique is most effective for ascending short, steep sections of terrain. (See figure 6-40.) Figure 6-40. Front pointing 6-118. Chapter 7 Navigation in Mountainous Terrain The goals, strategies, and tools available to Soldiers for navigation in mountainous terrain are no different from other types of terrain. However, mountainous terrain makes using those tools to stay on course much more difficult. Additionally, straying off course while navigating in this terrain can prove extremely hazardous and detrimental to mission success. The difficulty of planning routes and calculating movement timelines also increases significantly with the steepness and complexity of terrain. Soldiers and leaders who learn how to mitigate these challenges effectively can not only successfully navigate in mountainous terrain but also better use the terrain for cover and concealment. SECTION I - MILITARY LAND NAVIGATION IN NONTECHNICAL MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN 7-1. Navigation is the process of determining one's present position, locating a target objective, and selecting and following a route between these two points. Navigation consists of three distinct stages: orientation, navigation, and route finding. 7-2. Orientation is simply figuring out exactly where one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation. 7-3. Navigation determines the objective's location and the direction from the Soldier's starting point to the objective. The

one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation. 7-3. Navigation determines the objective's location and the direction from the Soldier's starting point to the objective. The same skills and equipment used in orientation are essential for good navigation. 7-4. Route finding is picking the best line of travel IAW METT-TC (I); mission, enemy, terrain and weather, troops and support available, time available, civil considerations, and informational considerations, and the commander's intent. Good route finding in mountainous terrain requires solid terrain analysis, clear priorities for route selection, an understanding of group members' levels of fitness and mobility skill, unit capabilities for technical movement, and mission-specific requirements. Examples of priorities for route selection are navigability of terrain, tactical advantage and disadvantage throughout the movement, concealment throughout, fatigue reduction, and required speed of movement. 7-5. Perhaps the single, most important factor in navigation through mountainous terrain is the ability to identify and analyze terrain. Navigators must be able to create an accurate mental model of the terrain to be moved through from a map or satellite imagery. The more skilled they are at this, the more effective they will

to identify and analyze terrain. Navigators must be able to create an accurate mental model of the terrain to be moved through from a map or satellite imagery. The more skilled they are at this, the more effective they will be at avoiding hazards, selecting tactically advantageous or concealed routes, and planning paths that minimize fatigue. This ability can only be developed effectively through route planning and movement in such terrain. Skill at land navigation in level terrain does not necessarily translate to skill in mountainous terrain. (See TC 3-25.26 for more information on general navigation techniques.) The following equipment should be considered for use when planning for or navigating in mountainous terrain: * Maps and protractors. * Imagery (satellite, aerial, or surface taken). * Compasses. * Altimeters. * GPS devices. MAPS AND PROTRACTORS 7-7. Ideal topographical maps for mountain navigation are those of sufficient scale and detail to depict terrain features accurately. This eliminates the conversion step usually required when obtaining navigational azimuths, thereby reducing time and probability of math errors. Information gathered during reconnaissance can often be inaccurate or incomplete once in the terrain and requires quick decision making and problem-solving ability. 7-65. Keep established landmarks in sight and move through terrain that allows for protection when and where fall hazards exist. Prioritize ridges and buttresses rather than faces and gullies when possible. This reduces exposure to rockfall and keeps Soldiers in position to observe the surrounding terrain. Gullies often look easier but are more difficult to assess and have looser terrain and generally more objective hazard. 7-66. A common route-finding mistake is climbing rock that appears easy but is loose or does not offer solid anchors or good options for protection, when other options are available. Another is misinterpreting the difficulty level of the terrain and climbing to the

route-finding mistake is climbing rock that appears easy but is loose or does not offer solid anchors or good options for protection, when other options are available. Another is misinterpreting the difficulty level of the terrain and climbing to the point where reversing direction becomes too difficult. Recognizing when one is "off route" early in the process is the key to avoiding serious injuries and major time delays. Any of these mistakes, when combined, can quickly lead to mission failure. 7-67. Soldiers must have experience with both success and failure when navigating in technical terrain to build the foundation of experience required to be effective on complex missions in the mountains. Time spent focused on planning, analyzing terrain, and executing technical movements while managing risk is invaluable to both the individual Soldiers and the unit. 7-68. Chapter 8 Knot Tying and Rope Management The rope is a vital piece of equipment to the mountaineer. It is used to address many of the problems and hazards encountered in the mountains. When climbing, rappelling, or building rope installations, the mountaineer must know how to utilize and maintain this equipment. Misuse can cause serious injury or death. This chapter discusses equipment, terminology, knots, hitches, rope management techniques, care, and maintenance. SECTION I - TYPES OF ROPE, WEBBING, AND CARABINERS 8-1. Mountaineering equipment is engineered to be lightweight but strong enough to provide a wide margin of safety. Each item is tested to high standards. In most cases, user error is to blame when this equipment fails. Soldiers should regularly check and inspect mountaineering equipment. Equipment should be replaced when there is any obvious damage, or it has exceeded the manufacturer's lifecycle recommendation. 8-2. All mountaineering equipment used in training should be constructed and tested to a recognized standard. The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, or Union des International Alpine Association (UIAA), is the certifying body that defines the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment. This safety commission develops the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment recognized throughout the world.

International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, or Union des International Alpine Association (UIAA), is the certifying body that defines the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment. This safety commission develops the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment recognized throughout the world. In Europe, the European Conformity, or Conformité Européene (CE), and the European Committee for Standardization establish standards across all industries. They publish standards that align with the UIAA standards for all climbing and mountaineering equipment produced in Europe. The United States has no specific standards, but American manufacturers have their equipment tested to receive UIAA certification. Any equipment used for mountaineering should be marked with either the UIAA safety label or the CE standard that it meets. ROPES AND CORDS 8-3. Ropes and cords are Soldiers' lifelines in the mountains. Soldiers should understand the types of ropes and cords and their applications. All ropes and cords used in mountaineering and climbing today are constructed with the same basic configuration. The construction technique is referred to as a kernmantle rope, which is a rope constructed with a load-bearing core of twisted synthetic fibers and a protective outer sheath of interwoven synthetic fibers. Chapter 8 8-4. There are many types of fibers and ropes that each have unique characteristics, making them suitable for specific tasks. The two main categories of rope are static and dynamic. Military mountaineers need to be able to differentiate between the two and know how each rope should be used. STATIC ROPE 8-5. A static rope is a kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and anchor systems construction. It has a core (kern) that is laid straight, giving it low stretch (2 to 8 percent). They are constructed with a tightly woven sheath (mantle) and are more durable than dynamic ropes. Static ropes are preferred for rappelling, rescue operations, load hauling, and rope installations. They should never be used in situations where the rope is shock loaded (for example, lead climbing). Typical diameter for static rope is between 9 and 11 millimeters (mm). Static rope is issued in 600 feet (183 meters) spools. While the minimum tensile strength for static ropes for military use is 4,500 pounds, the recommended working load is often 25 percent of the actual strength of that rope. The tensile strength for the 9.5 mm-issued low-stretch kernmantle rope

spools. While the minimum tensile strength for static ropes for military use is 4,500 pounds, the recommended working load is often 25 percent of the actual strength of that rope. The tensile strength for the 9.5 mm-issued low-stretch kernmantle rope is approximately 6,000 pounds. The length needed is dependent on the specific task being conducted. A 45-meter (150 feet) static has been the standard military length since the introduction of nylon ropes, but some tasks or obstacles may require a longer rope. The length of rope over 100 meters is a challenge to carry and manage. 8-6. The military purchases black static ropes to prevent a static rope from being mistaken for a climbing rope; however, static ropes are manufactured in all colors and patterns. A rope of unknown history or construction should not be used for any application. DYNAMIC ROPE (CLIMBING ROPE) 8-7. A dynamic rope is a kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect climbers from fall injuries. All climbing should be protected with dynamic ropes. Even short falls on static rope can cause serious injury. Standards for climbing ropes are established by the UIAA, and all climbing ropes should be certified. 8-8.

Standards for climbing ropes are established by the UIAA, and all climbing ropes should be certified. 8-8. The climbing ropes issued in the assault climbing team kits (ACTKs) are 60-meters long but can be cut shorter to meet mission or training requirements. Military climbing ropes are usually produced with olive drab or tan sheaths. CORD 8-9. Cord is thinner in diameter than rope. A carabiner is a D-shaped or oval-shaped metal link, with one spring-hinged side, that is used in mountaineering as a connector between soft materials and to capture a freely running rope. A carabiner is one of the most versatile pieces of equipment available to the mountaineer. This simple piece of gear is the critical connection between anchors, ropes, and mountaineers. (See figure 8-4.) 8-14. Most carabiners are constructed of aluminum. Carabiners are produced in several different shapes. Oval carabiners were once popular for general mountaineering because their symmetry makes them good for many purposes. Most carabiners used today are offset D-shaped carabiners, which offer the best compromise of weight to strength and ease of clipping and racking. (See figure 8-4.) 152 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

When using a carabiner, care should be taken to avoid cross loading the carabiner across the gate and spine and to avoid tri-loading. (See figure 8-5, page 154.) 8-16. There are two types of carabiners used in mountaineering: the locking carabiner and the nonlocking carabiner. LOCKING CARABINERS 8-17. Locking carabiners feature a barrel-shaped sleeve that prevents the gate from opening. They are used where an accidental carabiner opening could cause system failure. Any live load should be attached to an anchor with a locking carabiner. Locking carabiners are used for rappel hook ups, personal safeties, and the primary attachments in most rope systems. SECTION II - BASIC TERMINOLOGY 8-19. Understanding basic terminology is important when learning how to tie knots. The terms explained in this section are the most common in military mountaineering. (See figure 8-6, page 156.) RUNNING END 8-20. A running end is the loose or working end of the rope. STANDING END 8-21. The standing end is the static, stationary, or nonworking end of the rope. 154 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Knot Tying and Rope Management BIGHT 8-22. A bight of rope is a bend in the rope in which the standing end is parallel to the running end and the rope does not cross itself. LOOP 8-23. A loop is a bend of the rope in which the rope crosses itself. When the running end crosses over the top of the standing end, it is an overhand loop. When the running end crosses under the standing end, it is an underhand loop. TURN 8-24. A turn wraps around an object, providing 360° contact. ROUND TURN 8-25. A round turn wraps around an object one and one-half times so that the running and standing end are parallel. A round turn is used to hold an anchor or knot in place. HALF HITCH 8-26. A half hitch is a turn with the running end crossing over the standing end. TAIL 8-27. The tail is the excess portion of the running end of the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A safety knot is a backup knot tied to

the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A safety knot is a backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose. DRESSING 8-28. Dressing a knot is arranging all the knot parts, removing unnecessary kinks, twists, and slack so that all rope parts of the knot are secured and tight. SETTING 8-29. Setting a knot is removing all unnecessary slack from the knot. This ensures that the knot is tight and minimizes the chances of the knot becoming untied. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 155

Chapter 8 Figure 8-6. Examples of rope-tying terminology SECTION III - KNOT TYING AND CONSIDERATIONS 8-30. The term knot is commonly used to describe numerous categories. A knot is the fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some purpose. Sometimes it is referred to as a "hard knot" since its condition will remain intact until actively untied. Knots are self-contained and self-supporting and do not need another object or rope to maintain its integrity. Hitches are not considered knots. Yet, for simplicity, they are generalized into a single category. Knots should never be considered permanent. It is possible that they can loosen or become less secure under certain conditions. Knots should be inspected regularly. Many knots can accomplish the same task; therefore, it is important to understand these considerations when choosing the appropriate knot to tie. TYPES OF KNOTS 8-31. There are several broad types of knots that are used in mountaineering. Military mountaineers should be familiar with the following types and terms at a minimum. BENDS 8-32. Bends are used to join the ends of rope, cord, or webbing. When tied correctly, they are

of knots that are used in mountaineering. Military mountaineers should be familiar with the following types and terms at a minimum. BENDS 8-32. Specific joining knots should be used for certain situations and applications. Take care to learn the purpose of each joining knot and to have a clear understanding of where, when, and why to use each one. HITCHES 8-33. Hitches are like knots but are tied around another object or rope. A friction hitch is a type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned. Friction hitches grip the rope while under load, but they can be moved along the rope when unloaded. There are several friction hitches, each with different applications. Using the wrong friction hitch can be dangerous or create additional problems. LOOP KNOTS 8-35. Loop knots are used to create fixed or adjustable loops in rope or webbing. Some loops are directional to prevent the distortion of a knot when loaded. SPECIALTY KNOTS 8-36. These knots do not fit the above criteria but are still useful to know. They may only serve one specific purpose for mountaineering. KNOT TYING CONSIDERATIONS 8-37. There are several factors to consider when selecting knots for use or training. Military mountaineers do not need to be able to tie every possible knot that can be used in mountaineering. They just need to be able to tie an appropriate knot for each application they may face in their duties. When selecting knots for use in

to be able to tie every possible knot that can be used in mountaineering. They just need to be able to tie an appropriate knot for each application they may face in their duties. When selecting knots for use in mountaineering rigging, selecting simpler knots that are easier to tie, untie, and inspect are preferable to complex specialty knots, even if the complex knot is a little more effective. When considering teaching knot tying techniques to Soldiers and new military mountaineers, knots that are easier to teach and learn are preferred, as are multipurpose knots. Ultimately, the number and complexity of knots that military mountaineers may need to be proficient with increases as the scope and complexity of their technical mountaineering responsibilities and duties increase. Knot Tying and Rope Management SECTION IV - ROPES: PREPARATION, CARE, INSPECTION, COILING, CARRYING, AND THROWING 8-127. The service life of a rope depends on the frequency of use, applications (rappelling, climbing, rope installations), speed of descent, surface abrasion, terrain, climate, and quality of maintenance. Ropes may fail if misused, placed over sharp edges, or not properly inspected prior to use. PREPARING ROPES 8-128. The mountaineer must select the proper rope for the task to be accomplished according to type, diameter, length, and breaking strength. It is important to prepare all ropes before departing on a mission. Avoid rope preparation in the field. PACKAGING 8-129. New rope comes from the manufacturer in different configurations, boxed on a spool in various lengths, or coiled and bound in some manner. New ropes should be carefully unspooled or uncoiled to avoid kinks and prevent tangling. Coil 8-130. A coil is a secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling. Precut 8-131. Precut ropes are usually packaged in a protective cover, such as plastic. SECURING THE ENDS OF ROPE 8-132. If still on a spool, the rope must be cut to the desired length. All ropes fray at the ends unless

8-131. Precut ropes are usually packaged in a protective cover, such as plastic. SECURING THE ENDS OF ROPE 8-132. If still on a spool, the rope must be cut to the desired length. All ropes fray at the ends unless they are bound or seared. Both static and dynamic rope ends are secured in the same manner. The ends must be heated to the melting point to attach the inner core strands to the outer sheath. By fusing the two together, the sheath cannot slide backward or forward. Ensure that this is only done to the ends of the rope. If the rope is exposed to extreme temperatures, the sheath could be weakened, along with the inner core, reducing overall tensile strength. The ends may also be dipped in enamel or lacquer for further protection. CARE AND MAINTENANCE 8-133. The rope is a climber's lifeline. The rope must be maintained and used properly. Climbers should use the following general guidelines when handling ropes: * While in use, do not allow the rope to touch sharp edges. Rope is cut more easily when under tension. If the rope must be used over a sharp edge, pad the edge for protection and

when handling ropes: * While in use, do not allow the rope to touch sharp edges. Rope is cut more easily when under tension. If the rope must be used over a sharp edge, pad the edge for protection and inspect often. * Never allow one rope to continuously run over another. The friction causes the nylon to melt. * Never leave a rope knotted or tightly stretched for longer than necessary. Doing so reduces the strength and life of the rope over time. * UV radiation (sunlight) tends to deteriorate nylon over long periods. This becomes important if rope installations are left in place for months. * Do not step on or drag ropes on the ground unnecessarily. Small particles of dirt grind between the inner strands slowly cutting them. * All ropes should be washed periodically to remove dirt and grit and rinsed thoroughly. Army-issued rope washes are made from short pieces of modified pipe that connect to any faucet. Pinholes within the pipe force water to circulate around and scrub the rope as the Soldier slowly feeds it through the washer. * Ropes should not be stored wet. Dry wet ropes by uncoiling and hanging them in

any faucet. Pinholes within the pipe force water to circulate around and scrub the rope as the Soldier slowly feeds it through the washer. * Ropes should not be stored wet. Dry wet ropes by uncoiling and hanging them in large loops off the ground. Never dry a rope with high heat or in direct sunlight. * When not in use, ropes should be loosely coiled and hung on wooden pegs rather than nails or other metal objects. Storage areas should be relatively cool with low-humidity levels to prevent mildew 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 189

Chapter 9 Anchor Selection and Construction Understanding anchors is an important fundamental that must be understood early in the path to becoming a military mountaineer. An anchor is the point where manufactured equipment for mountaineering meets the surface of the earth. Great varieties of natural features are found in different operational environments that a Soldier could use to construct an anchor. Anchors are found in all rope systems and are built in many ways. This chapter gives Soldiers the tools to assess terrain for the suitability of anchor construction for a wide variety of rope systems. This chapter also exposes Soldiers to the principles of anchor construction that ensure they are building solid anchors in a wide variety of terrain for many different purposes. Anchor selection in mountainous terrain requires a certain degree of knowledge and substantial experience. Most mountaineering accidents occur at the anchor. Inexperienced Soldiers should stick to selecting anchor features that are obviously stronger than necessary and choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar. choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar. SECTION I - GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT 9-1. An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. It is a point in the operational environment, which a rope installation is attached, providing more than enough resistance to a directional pull. Rope systems can be used for moving casualties and equipment. Some, like rappels or fixed ropes, are used for aiding movement. Technical rope systems provide the tools for addressing many of the challenges posed by mountainous terrain. Anchor selection and evaluation together form the foundation of all systems. 9-2. Considerations for selecting a natural feature to construct an anchor are its location and ability to resist any forces that are placed upon it. The anchor should be above any intended rope pathways. This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform

This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform to work on. In other situations, such as setting a top rope, it is best to have the anchor near the edge. This aspect of anchor building can be challenging as the strength of natural features, such as rocks, trees, roots, and boulders; can be difficult to judge. Soldiers must err on the side of caution and leave no doubt that an anchor is strong enough for its intended purpose. If there is any doubt about a single-point anchor's strength or security, then additional anchor components should be constructed and incorporated until sufficient strength and security are achieved to ensure that anchor failure cannot occur. The strength of an anchor should never be in question. 9-3. Anchors in mountaineering should be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Pitons still have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely strong and secure anchor option when placed properly. Chapter 9 BOLTS 9-39. A bolt is a type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached. Bolts are often used in fixed-rope installations and in aid climbing where cracks are not available. Bolts provide one of the most secure means of establishing protection. 9-40. Some bolts have rings attached for easy retrievable rappelling, clip-in points for top rope climbing, chains to aid in establishing tope rope climbing anchors, or other special-purpose attachment points. 9-41. There are two primary types of bolts: expansion bolts and glue-in bolts. Both involve drilling a hole into a rock face, cleaning out dust and debris, and inserting a bolt. The difference is in how the bolt is secured in the hole: * Expansion bolts use a sleeve that expands as it is tightened. The sleeve expands against the walls of the hole to prevent it from coming out. (See figure 9-16.) * Glue-in bolts are held in place by a high-strength adhesive. Glue-in bolts are used in softer, porous rock, such as sandstone. Delicate rock, like sandstone, may not be strong enough to support expansion bolts. Its

Any bolting should be done with the consensus of the climbing community. 9-45. PLACEMENT 9-50. The principles of placing chocks are to find a crack with a constriction at some point, place a chock of appropriate size above and behind the constriction, and set the chock by gently jerking down. Maximum surface contact with a tight fit is critical. Chocks are usually good for a single direction of pull. 9-51. Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. When selecting a chock, choose one that has as much surface area as possible in contact with the rock. A chock resting on one small crystal or point of rock is likely to be unsafe. Anchor Selection and Construction 9-54. Chocks must be lightly tugged on to set them so that they do not fall out of placement. Weighting the placement helps to keep the protection in position. A carabiner often provides enough weight. CAMMING DEVICES 9-55. Camming devices are designed for building anchors in parallel-sided cracks where chocks are ineffective. There are several different types, but they all work by changing from a downward force to an outward force when loaded. This force creates enough friction that the device cannot move, even when no constriction in the crack is present. Camming devices increase force on surrounding rock as downward force is applied. Due to this, care should be taken to inspect the security of the rock on which they are placed. 9-56. Camming devices become even more secure when placed above a constriction. If the lobes slip during loading, they cannot exit the crack. 9-57. Cams are the most used camming devices in mountaineering. They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types

They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types of cams, the modern design consists of two sets of lobes that oppose each other and rotate from one or two axles, connected to a trigger mechanism on a single, flexible stem that runs perpendicular to the axle. Attached to the axle is a presewn connection sling. They are designed to work in parallel-sided cracks where a chock would just slide down. 9-59. Cams come in a wide variety of sizes to fit cracks from 0.5 inches to over 21 inches. Each unit has an expansion range that enables it to function properly within a certain width of cracks. It may be necessary to carry many sizes depending upon the route, mission, and intended use. Most come with color-coded slings to help the user select the correct size for use. 9-60. Three quality camming devices equalized together are required to establish an adequate anchor. An exception is two large camming devices perfectly placed in solid rock with constrictions below them.

The disadvantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below: * They can wiggle or walk out of proper placement, resulting in a compromised anchor, or in a stuck camming device that is difficult or

the surrounding rock. 9-62. PLACEMENT 9-63. To place cams, find a uniform, parallel spot in the crack where the rock is clean and solid. Retract the lobes by pulling back on the trigger. The ice screw is the most common type of ice protection. An ice screw is a threaded tubular screw with teeth on the end. Chapter 9 9-75. The security of an ice screw is determined by the quality of the ice in which it is placed. The thicker and denser the ice is, the stronger it is. Thinner ice, aerated ice, or ice with air pockets is weak; mountaineers should avoid this sort of ice. Deep, thick ice is generally bluish in color, while ice that has air pockets is often white in color. It takes significant experience to judge the strength of ice, but even a novice can learn much about ice quality by the resistance felt when placing the ice screw. Air pockets are felt as a reduction in resistance. The more resistance, the denser the ice. The longer the core grows as it is screwed in, typically the better the ice. (See figure 9-23.) Evaluate the integrity of the ice structure. If possible, avoid fracture lines, the apex of ice bulges, and ice blocks that are not attached to a main flow. Figure 9-23. Chapter 10 Rope Systems for Climbing There is an inherent risk to moving in the mountains. Much of the terrain is high consequence, where a misjudged foothold, a loose rock, a slip, trip, or fall can kill. However, troops fighting in the mountains are often exposed to greater risk by not being able to move through the terrain. Examples exist throughout history. Modern examples include the assaults on Riva Ridge and Monte la Difensa in Italy, both examples of failed conventional assaults, where defensive positions in the heights were taken by assaults through more difficult terrain. More recently, the Indians retaking hilltops in the Kargil Conflict display all the same principles. Successful offensive operations in the mountains require troops who can move in difficult terrain and under poor conditions. The alternative is costly, often unsuccessful attacks where the defenders hold significant tactical advantage. To manage the risk involved with movement through these types of terrain, Soldiers must be trained in a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I - RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one

a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I - RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one hazard increase the exposure to another. Installing or using ropes to protect against a fall increases movement time and increases the exposure to compromise by enemy forces. MANAGING RISK 10-2. Managing risk in the mountains is a dynamic process, where the most appropriate measures for managing risk change with the terrain and situation. 10-3. Control measures target either the consequence or the likelihood of an incident. Protective equipment, such as a helmet to protect against rockfall, only reduces the consequence. The likelihood of being hit by rockfall is addressed by avoiding areas of loose rock and routing Soldiers so that they do not travel above one another. REDUCING THE LIKELIHOOD OF A FALL 10-4. The mountaineer has several technical tools for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. SECTION III - BELAYED CLIMBING 10-13. A belay is a system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier's fall should one occur. This section will discuss an overview of various strategies for using ropes and belays. TYPES OF BELAYED CLIMBING 10-14. When terrain is too dangerous to move unroped, a team will transition to belayed climbing. Belayed climbing is usually done in a party of two, with each climber tied into one end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing.
