Chapter 10 LEAD CLIMBING 10-16. As military mountaineers progress, they are later introduced to lead climbing. Lead climbing is climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall protection with a belayer located below. When lead climbing, one climber leads climbs, placing protection and clipping the rope through it as they go. The belayer (sometimes referred to as the second) belays and is prepared to catch a fall. Lead climbers climb to another secure stance, build a solid anchor, and then belay second climbers as they climb to the new stance. Each length of climbing is called a pitch, which is a section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length (60 meters) on easy ice and snow. In more broken rock, it may be just 10 to 15 meters, to minimize rope drag and aid communication. 10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. The second has a top rope unless the route traverses. The overall security of the team is good. The team always has a solid attachment, and the belays can be placed in sheltered stances, with solid anchors. (See section V for more information on lead climbing.) 10-18. Most climbers will protect themselves with belays in 5th-class terrain. In 3rd- or 4th-class terrain, in darkness or bad weather, belayed climbing is the most conservative strategy for protecting the team and provides the greatest margin of safety. AID CLIMBING 10-19. Simul-climbing is a belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection. It is a variation of belayed climbing, where leaders continue to climb rather than stopping to belay the second. Second climbers climb simultaneously, removing protection as they go. Leaders continue to climb while trying to keep a few pieces of protection between the two climbers at all times. If one falls, they may pull their teammate off their stance, but they will be caught eventually, counterbalanced through the protection with the other climber. Simul-climbing is faster than belayed climbing and useful for covering easy ground quickly. (See figure 10-3, page 240.) Simul-climbing provides more security than soloing. Climbers may find it necessary to shorten ropes between 20 and 30 meters to help with communication and prevent rope drag. 10-22. When both climbers are moving together, both share the consequence of a fall. Climbers should only use simul-climbing where a fall is unlikely and with partners of similar ability. Short roping is used by more experienced mountaineers for protecting less experienced Soldiers in easy but exposed terrain. In a training environment, safety and conservative decision making must be the primary focus. As military mountaineers progress in their training, they may be exposed to alpine terrain above tree line. Weather and environmental hazards can pose a greater threat than falling. Each strategy for protecting the movement of the team is a compromise that should match the difficulty of terrain and the consequence of a fall. It should not expose the team to greater risk from another hazard. For combat operations, military mountaineers may need to compromise on protection and belays even further. Speed, stealth, and the ability to react are critical if enemy contact is expected. SECTION IV - TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-33. It has the advantage of requiring no extra equipment and maintaining a sufficient level of friction to stop a fall with the brake strand in a variety of positions. Its main disadvantage is that it twists and kinks the rope. * Place a locking carabiner into the tie-in portion of the harness. Lock the carabiner. * To take in rope, grasp the brake strand with the brake hand a few inches away from the Munter hitch and with the thumb pointed up. below the guide hand. With the guide hand, grasp both ropes just above the brake hand, and then slide the brake hand back down to its original place, a few inches from the Munter hitch. The hitch creates enough friction for the belayer to easily hold the climber's body weight. The brake position for the Munter hitch is with the brake strand and the load strand parallel. * Never let go of the brake strand. * To lower the climber back down, place both hands on the brake strand and feed the rope slowly back through the Munter hitch until the climber is safely on the ground. The procedures for conducting a lead climb with a group of two are relatively simple. The most experienced individual is the lead climber or leader. Leaders are responsible for selecting the route. They must ensure that the route is well within their climbing ability and that of the second climber ("second"). The lead climber carries most of the climbing equipment to place protection along the route and set up the next belay. The leader must also ensure that the second has the necessary equipment, such as a chock pick, to remove any protection that the leader may place. 10-91. The leader is responsible for emplacing protection frequently enough and in such a manner that if either the leader or the second should fall, their fall is neither long enough nor hard enough to result in injury. The leader must also ensure that the rope is routed so that it can run freely through the protection placements, thus minimizing friction, or rope drag. 10-92.

objects in the swinging path of the second. REDUCING ROPE DRAG; USING RUNNERS 10-96. No matter how direct the route, the climber often encounters problems with rope drag through the protection positions. Rope drag is caused when there are exaggerated changes in direction of the rope between carabiners attached to protection that creates excessive friction. Minimal rope drag is an inconvenience; severe rope drag may pull the climber off balance, inducing a fall. When belaying the second, rope drag can be mistaken for the climber, causing the belayer to not take in the necessary slack. This can potentially result in a serious fall. To prevent this, the placements should be extended by using runners, when necessary, so the rope creates a smooth, almost straight line as it passes through the carabiners. (See figure 10-16.) Do this by attaching an appropriate-length runner to the protection to extend the rope connection in the necessary direction. The runner is attached to the protection while the rope is clipped into a carabiner at the opposite end of the runner. Extending placements with runners allows the climber to vary the route slightly while the rope continues to run in a relatively straight line. 260 TC

Clip the climbing rope into a point of protection by reaching down and grabbing the rope between the thumb and index finger. Use the middle finger to stabilize the carabiner at the protection or runner, and use the thumb and index finger to clip the rope in. Recreational climbers typically do all their clipping while hanging onto rock holds as much as they can; however, as a Soldier not worried about preserving the free climbing style, simply grab the point of protection and hang onto it while clipping the rope and runner into it. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training. Lead climbing training is particularly demanding of trainers and supervisors. For inexperienced climbers, a 2:1 ratio is often required. Chapter 10 SECTION VI - ALPINE BELAY TECHNIQUES 10-118. In broken alpine terrain, with secure stances, and no chance of second climbers falling and hanging from a belay, hasty techniques may provide adequate protection for the team. Safety should never be compromised for the sake of speed. Use of standard belay techniques should be used if there is any question as to security. BODY BELAYS 10-119. Body belays can sometimes be used on short sections of less steep terrain where a fall is unlikely and there is a good, braced belay stance of which to take advantage. To create a body belay, simply run the rope around the body at the waist to create friction, with the chest facing the direction of pull. The load rope is at one hip and the brake strand is in the opposite side hand. To take in rope, pull in on the load rope with the guide hand and out with the brake hand. Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the

Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the sitting or standing position; however, the sitting position offers a lower center of gravity and is preferred. It can also be used with an anchor or without. The advantage of the body belay is its speed and simplicity for belaying short sections where a climber is moving quickly. However, there are disadvantages as well. Because the force of a fall is dissipated as friction against belayers' bodies, serious rope burns can occur to the body and hands, possibly causing them to lose control of the belay. It also generates less braking force and causes more slippage than other techniques, causing the climber to fall farther. For this reason, it is only used on low-angle easy terrain. The belayer must have a good, braced position and must keep the rope tight. (See figure 10-21.) 268 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Rope Systems for Climbing Figure 10-21. Hip belay SHOULDER BELAY 10-120. A shoulder belay is a way to add a level of friction to the rope as the belayer pulls it tight with a climber below. The shoulder belay shares many of the advantages and disadvantages listed above for the body belay. The level of friction created with this method is relatively low and should only be used on short steps where there is no risk of the climber hanging from the belay in a fall. A classic example of terrain where the shoulder belay is appropriate is a short, steep step where the belayer can stand directly above the climber below. The rope is routed under the arm, over the opposite shoulder, and down to the opposite hand and is kept tight with the climber below. The belayer's body creates friction on the rope and acts as the anchor at the same time. A shoulder belay is fast to create, but it is only suitable on rare occasions. (See figure 10-22, page 270.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 269

The natural feature must be solid and not have sharp edges. Terrain belays are an effective means of belaying a climbing partner, but they require good judgement. When using a boulder or horn of rock, the belayer must ensure the rope will not slide off the rock in the event of a fall and that the rock is wedged securely. Trees are another good example of a natural object that can be used as a terrain belay. (See chapter 9 for more information on tree selection.) (See figure 10-23.) 270 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Chapter 11 Fixed Ropes Fixed ropes are an important part of military mountaineering as they facilitate the movement of Soldiers through rugged terrain. Fixed ropes allow large groups of Soldiers to safely access terrain that provides tactical advantage over the enemy. They have proven useful in past conflicts. During World War II, they were successfully used during Operation Neptune (commonly referred to as D-day) and the famous assault on Riva Ridge by the 10th Mountain Division. Proficiency in using fixed ropes allows units to overcome mobility limitations and, therefore, achieve greater lethality in mountainous terrain. SECTION I - BASIC FIXED-ROPE TECHNIQUES 11-1. A fixed rope is any rope system attached to at least one anchor that can be used to improve security and efficiency of movement through difficult terrain that subjects Soldiers to a fall hazard. They can be used for ascending, descending, or traversing across steep terrain in which a fall hazard exists. They may simply provide Soldiers with a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement

a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement of small teams to large units. They allow units to overcome mobility limitations and access tactically advantageous terrain. FIXED-ROPE CONSIDERATIONS 11-2. Fixed ropes should be used whenever a group of Soldiers cannot move safely through a section of terrain unroped. Fixed ropes are usually the most efficient means of protecting groups larger than team sized, especially if the groups have not received advanced military mountaineering training. Common factors contributing to the necessity of building fixed ropes are fall hazard, slippery surfaces, limited visibility, heavy loads, low mobility skills, and fatigue. 11-3. The two basic types of fixed-rope systems are simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate anchors. Both types have applications in every class of terrain. Simple fixed ropes are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more

are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more Soldiers to move on them simultaneously and the path to change directions. Each type is determined by route and availability of anchors along it, the number of Soldiers to use the system, and the type of available equipment to attach to it. 11-4. All types of fixed ropes are built from the top down over, or through, terrain obstacles. However, fixed rope installation teams may need to ascend terrain using other techniques prior to building a fixed-rope system. (See chapter 10.) 11-5. Units planning to use fixed ropes must establish installation teams capable of locating routes, moving safely through various terrain obstacles, and building a variety of installations. They should be led by advanced military mountaineers but may be assisted by basic military mountaineers. These teams should be experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them. 11-6. These teams should be experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them. 11-6. In a tactical environment, any terrain that requires a fixed rope should be considered a VDA, which is steep terrain that puts a unit moving through it at significant tactical disadvantage. The process for establishing even the simplest fixed rope comes at the cost of time and exposure to enemy attack. Adequate security must be established prior to deploying the installation team. In complex terrain, security teams may need to be adjusted or leap-frogged forward if fixed-rope systems cover large pieces of terrain. Emplacing security teams in a complex terrain may require high-mobility skills as well as substantial time. Typically, it is best to approach fixed-rope terrain from above because security is more easily established on higher 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 275

SIMPLE FIXED ROPES 11-7. A simple fixed rope is a rope that is anchored at the top of steep terrain that can be used to increase safety or efficiency of movement up or down. The method of anchoring the rope is determined by anchor features available but can be as simple as a bowline tied to a tree or as complex as a multipoint anchor established with rock-climbing gear. The principal benefit of simple, fixed ropes is their simplicity and speed of construction. 11-8. Simple fixed ropes are typically established by one mountaineer climbing the obstacle, dragging a rope, and then anchoring it at the top. They can also be established by approaching the top of a steep obstacle by some other means, anchoring a rope, and lowering the other end down for others to use. 11-9. end down for others to use. 11-9. Some important considerations for using simple fixed-rope systems are that they must follow a path straight up the terrain feature, the attachment technique is appropriate to reduce fall risk, and they allow for a large enough loading and unloading platform to manage the site safely. Using a friction hitch or mechanical progress capture to attach to the rope provides increased security during movement. EASY TERRAIN 11-10. Short 2nd- or 3rd-class slopes with low fall consequence can be negotiated using simple fixed ropes without the necessity of attaching to the rope. Soldiers using the fixed rope simply grasp the rope with the thumb downward and use it in a hand-over-hand fashion to assist with balance. (See figure 11-1.) This technique is appropriate when there is an increased likelihood of fall but low consequence. Usually this means short slopes that Soldiers could easily negotiate normally, but slippery conditions, fatigue, or heavy loads increase the chance of a fall. Fixed Ropes MODERATE TERRAIN 11-11. Short sections of steep 3rd or 4th class with higher fall consequence can be negotiated by attaching to simple fixed ropes with a progress capture, such as a prusik or other mechanical rope-grabbing device. This technique requires Soldiers to wear some type of harness. A significant drawback to this technique is that it takes a lot of time to move a group of Soldiers. Only one Soldier can move at a time on a rope, and time is lost during attachment and detachment. (See figure 11-2, page 278.) Prusik Technique 11-12. A common technique involves tying a prusik on the rope with a cordelette, then tying a fixed loop in the other end of the two tails. Clip the fixed loop to the harness with a locking carabiner. The optimum length of the attachment is one outstretched arm. 11-13. Ascend the fixed rope by using the legs to climb the slope and the rope as a handhold for balance, sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip. 11-14. The prusik technique is recommended only on simple fixed ropes without intermediate anchor points because friction hitches cannot be easily

a handhold for balance, sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip. 11-14. The prusik technique is recommended only on simple fixed ropes without intermediate anchor points because friction hitches cannot be easily or safely transitioned past intermediate anchors. Mechanical Ascender Technique 11-15. It is also possible to use a rope-grabbing device, such as a mechanical ascender, to create a progress capture for Soldiers moving on fixed ropes. These devices are easier and faster to use but require every Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has limited uses. They should be used when fixed rope ascents are planned for large groups in moderate terrain. 11-16. Mechanical ascenders are devices shaped like a handle that can be attached to a rope by means of a toothed cam. It can slide in one direction on a rope but not the other. When weighted, the camming mechanism activates and grips the rope. Soldiers can attach ascenders to their harness and slide them along fixed ropes during movement, capturing their progress and preventing a fall during a slip (see figure 11-2, page 278). Some are much lighter but are less easy to use. Moving on simple fixed ropes in terrain where significant sections are very steep or vertical requires rigging that is more complex. These rigging techniques provide secure attachment to the rope and aid movement up the rope. (See paragraphs 11-36 through 11-52, pages 282 through 286, for more information on ascending techniques.) FIXED ROPES WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS 11-20. Larger or more complex sections of steep terrain require fixed ropes with intermediate anchors to ensure adequate safety and efficiency of movement. This may involve various sections of 3rd, 4th, or even 5th-class terrain. The principal difference between simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate anchors is the use of intermediate anchor points to create independent sections and changes in direction of travel. This allows the movement route to follow the easiest, safest, and most efficient path. This type of fixed rope is commonly used along exposed ridges and narrow mountain passes. 11-21. Advanced or master military mountaineers with substantial experience are required to establish fixed ropes with intermediate anchors, but they can be assisted by basic military mountaineers. FIXED-ROPE CONSTRUCTION WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS 11-22. The primary guiding principles for building a fixed rope with intermediate anchors are that they provide adequate fall prevention while maximizing the speed at which Soldiers can move using them. Path 11-23. Establishing a fixed rope with intermediate anchors starts with thorough terrain analysis and route finding. When selecting a path for the rope, mountaineers must consider the anchor options available, difficulty of movement on the route, and any other objective hazards present. The characteristics of the Soldiers who use the fixed rope are also useful information. Particularly, what their mobility and technical skill levels are and what equipment they have for attaching to the rope. 278 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Intermediate Anchors 11-24. Terrain and vegetation determine the equipment mountaineers need to build the fixed rope. Heavily vegetated terrain or broken rocky terrain may only require cordelettes, slings, and carabiners. Slabby or steep rock faces require cams, nuts, and other lead climbing protection to build anchors. Intermediate anchors must be built robust enough to support the weight of a fall by the number of Soldiers who will move on each section at a given time. Two primary methods exist for use in steep terrain: the two personal safeties method and the ascender-carabiner method. Choosing between the two is a tradeoff between not carrying heavier single-purpose items and having more security during movement. The two personal safeties method requires no special equipment but cannot eliminate fall risk for a Soldier. The ascender-carabiner method prevents falling but requires each Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has little other use. The carabiners are then attached to the fixed rope. Always keep the two carabiners attached to the rope unless they move past an intermediate anchor. Chapter 11 FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-33. Fixed ropes are sometimes necessary for moving in vertical terrain during complex rescue operations or other special operations in permissive or nontactical environments. They are rarely practical for tactical operations, given their extreme exposure to enemy observation and direct fire. However, vertical terrain is not always avoidable during combat operations, and there are historical examples of their use during pivotal cliff assaults. Vertical terrain is the most extreme example of VDA. Soldiers moving on vertically fixed ropes require well-established overwatch security since they are totally exposed and can do little but ascend the fixed rope. 11-34. Moving on fixed ropes in vertical terrain requires Soldiers to possess the equipment and skills necessary to ascend rope, relying entirely on their attachment to it to prevent fall. Efficient ascending requires specialized equipment. CONSTRUCTING FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-35. Fixed ropes in vertical terrain are constructed in the same fashion as moderate terrain; however, they take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build the system top-down.

Weapon Management 11-51. Unless enemy attack is imminent, weapons should be slung to the rear, allowing Soldiers to scramble more easily in difficult terrain. Hard snow is especially easy to carve steps into and can allow Soldiers to move with less exertion on their calf muscles. Carving steps should be done first in steeper sections and, as time allows, in other areas too. Platforms can also be made where Soldiers are transitioning past intermediate anchors. If a Soldier can easily stand near an intermediate anchor, they can clip around it much faster. This greatly lessens the time required for the group to navigate terrain where objective hazards may be present. Etriers or Slings at Difficult Steps 11-53. The hanging of a sling or etrier (for use as a hand or foothold) where there is a difficult step can help reduce fall potential and increase speed of the group. An etrier is a short ladder that can be made from any piece of rope or cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. They also enable Soldiers to navigate challenging terrain in the dark, much easier than if they had to search for hand and foot placements. Fixed Ropes Figure 11-8. Etrier styles SECTION II - TYPES OF RAPPELLING 11-56. Rappelling is a method of descending steep terrain using a rope and a means of creating friction to control the rate of descent. This provides Soldiers with a safe way to descend terrain that would otherwise expose them to very high fall risks. 11-57. If the descent distance is greater than a rope length (for example, multipitch), multiple, simple fixed lines can be linked together with anchors at the top and bottom of each rope. Soldiers can then rappel from anchor to anchor and transition from rope to rope until they reach the ground. This method requires many resources and numerous personnel to establish and manage safely. 11-58. Small teams with fewer resources must use the one or two ropes they can carry to rappel the whole group from one anchor to a lower one, then retrieve the rope, and repeat the process until the ground is reached. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 287

Chapter 11 RAPPELLING FUNDAMENTALS 11-59. Rappelling is a quick method of descent, but it can be extremely dangerous. The dangers include anchor failure, equipment failure, and individual error. Carefully select anchors in a mountainous environment. In a mountain environment, take great care to load the anchor slowly and to ensure that no excessive stress is placed on the anchor. To ensure this, prohibit bounding while rappelling; Soldiers should slowly descend. Soldiers should avoid dragging their feet when moving backwards towards the edge as this causes rockfall. 11-60. Soldiers rappelling with weapons should sling them on the back or to the side when wearing packs. Soldiers carrying particularly heavy weapons, such as machine guns, sniper rifles, or mortars may need to strap them to the top of their pack and use additional techniques described below to make rappelling less difficult. RAPPEL SITE SELECTION 11-61. Selecting the rappel point depends on factors, such as mission, cover, route, anchor availability, and edge composition (for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier

(for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier and reduce the likelihood of Soldiers stumbling or falling. Stumbles and falls are likely to increase the risk of rope damage on sharp rock as well as increase force exerted on anchors. 11-63. Rappel sites with suitable loading and off-loading platforms should be selected. Ideally, they are flat and allow for anchoring far enough away from the edge that Soldiers do not need to be attached to an anchor to prevent accidentally falling off the edge. If this is impossible, use fixed-rope techniques described in section I when approaching the rappel point. A staging area large enough to hold the group in a safe place nearby is also desirable. INSTALLATION CONSIDERATIONS 11-64. The two major factors in deciding how to attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In

Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In an operational environment, or during advanced military mountaineering training, ropes must be retrievable. This is because there is presumably no other feasible way to negotiate the vertical obstacle, or the group would be using it. All people and equipment must rappel, and the rope must be recovered for future use. This means that the rope cannot be fixed to the top anchor when the last Soldier begins rappelling. 11-66. When training basic rappelling, retrieving ropes is not necessary. Appropriate rappel sites for inexperienced rappellers should include access between the top and bottom by some other safe means for set up and breakdown. This allows for a greater safety margin by using two fixed independent strands for rappel ropes. Not only does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical rappelling in an operational environment. 11-67. All rigging should be inspected by a qualified advanced military mountaineer, at a minimum. RETRIEVABLE RAPPELS 11-68. Retrievable rappels can be established using appropriate single-point anchors (such as a tree, boulder, horn of rock) using only the rope, or they can be attached to cordelettes, or webbing tied around the anchor feature. If other materials are used, then they cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-69. Multipoint anchors require additional materials to establish. This material cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-70. The minimum necessary equipment should be used in building retrievable rappel anchors. 288 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Half-Rope Length 11-71. The simplest and most common method is to just run one end of the rope around anchor feature, and then double back stack it until the middle of the rope is around the anchor feature. This ensures both strands are the same length. Tie a stopper knot at the bottom end with both strands leaving 12- to 18-inch tails. This prevents accidentally rappelling off the end of the rope. The ropes are then thrown or back stacked over the edge. 11-72. Sometimes the rope cannot be routed directly around the anchor. The rope can then be back stacked so that the middle of the rope passes through the attachment point for an anchor made from cordelette or webbing or clipped to it using a locking carabiner. 11-73. If a rope could be cut, it is possible to make the system redundant for all but the last rappeller. This system is established in the same manner as above, but once complete a BHK is tied close to the anchor with both strands. as above, but once complete a BHK is tied close to the anchor with both strands. This creates two fixed independent strands and adds redundancy to the system. Before the last Soldiers begin to rappel, they simply untie the BHK, and the system is retrievable again. Full-Length Rope 11-74. Full-length rappels require two standard-length ropes. Route the end of one rope around or through the anchor point and tie a flat double overhand with the ends of both ropes joining them. Double back stack the ropes and tie a stopper knot as described above. Using a flat overhand to join the rappel ropes reduces the likelihood of the knot being stuck in vegetation of rock features during retrieval. 11-75. Full-length rappels can be made redundant for all but the last rappeller in the same manner as is described above. Rappel Rope Retrieval 11-76. Once all Soldiers have reached the bottom and any stopper knots have been untied, the rope can be retrieved by pulling one strand. The other strand travels up to the anchor and falls. It is a good idea to get excess personnel away from the area prior to pulling in case any loose rocks are dislodged above. 11-77. When pulling the rope on a multipitch rappel, it is a good idea to route the end being pulled through the next anchor, so the rope is less likely to be dropped. RAPPELS WITH FIXED STRANDS 11-78. Whenever a threat of the installation rope being cut is identified, two fixed independent strands should be used. Two strands add redundancy and reduce the likelihood that a fall may occur in a cut rope incident. Installations with two fixed independent strands are typically the standard for rappelling training whether a hazard has been identified. Half-Rope Length 11-79. If using a single anchor, anchor the middle of the rope to it with a bowline knot. If using a preequalized multipoint anchor, tie a fixed loop in the middle of the rope, and attach it to the anchor with two opposing locking carabiners. Full-Rope Length

Situations may arise where the distance of anchors from each other, or the distance of the anchors from the rappel point, requires using a second rope to construct an anchor, or extend the anchor master point closer to the loading platform, allowing for the maximum amount of rope to be utilized for the rappel. In this case, tie a fixed loop with the top ends of both ropes, and clip it to the anchor system master point using two opposing locking carabiners. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 289

Chapter 11 RAPPEL INSTALLATION SPECIAL TECHNIQUES 11-82. There are a few problems that mountaineers should be prepared to solve related to rappelling. The common problems are damaged ropes, short ropes, and the threat of a rope being cut when retrievability is necessary. Damaged Rope 11-83. Ropes occasionally become damaged but may need to be used until they can be replaced following an operation. Mountaineers must be familiar with how to safely use damaged ropes for rappelling. 11-84. First, tie an overhand knot, isolating the damaged spot in the rope. The rope can then continue to be used for many mountaineering tasks. However, the knot in the rope prevents Soldiers from rappelling past. 11-85. If a retrievable rappel is necessary, the damaged rope can be used as follows. The rope is back stacked around the anchor as usual. A fixed bight is tied in the damaged strand near the anchor. That bight is then clipped to the nondamaged strand with a locking carabiner. When loaded, the carabiner fits snug to the anchor like a slip knot. (See figure 11-9.) Both strands of rope are thrown or back stacked off the cliff. 11-86. Soldiers can then rig for rappel using only the

locking carabiner. When loaded, the carabiner fits snug to the anchor like a slip knot. (See figure 11-9.) Both strands of rope are thrown or back stacked off the cliff. 11-86. Soldiers can then rig for rappel using only the nondamaged strand and descend the obstacle. Note. Rappelling on a single strand creates less friction. 11-87. Once all Soldiers have rappelled, the damaged strand, or tagline, can be pulled to retrieve the rope. The nondamaged strand travels up through the carabiner, around the anchor and back down. More care should be taken when pulling the rope because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique. Sometimes a group may only have one rope that is not long enough to reach the bottom of a cliff, and the rope cannot be retrieved because the cliff is taller than a half-rope length. 11-89. If the group has enough cordelettes or shorter sections of rope, it can solve the problem. To do so, one end of the rope is lowered until it is on the ground. Cordelettes are then joined by a single strand to the other end until they reach the ground. 11-90. The installation is then rigged to be retrievable with a tagline (as described in paragraphs 11-83 through 11-87, page 290). Soldiers can then rappel on the strand of static rope. Take more care when pulling the rope because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique. 11-91. Small units can use this technique to reduce the weight of rope they need to carry. units can use this technique to reduce the weight of rope they need to carry. Threat of Cut Rope Using a Retrievable System 11-92. Some situations may require a retrievable rappel, but a threat to the rope is identified (such as sharp rock or falling rock hazard) that cannot be mitigated by simply padding an edge. This problem can be resolved by one of two methods. 11-93. The first involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then attaching a tube-style device and locking carabiner tight to the anchor. This effectively fixes both strands. All but the last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed strands. The last Soldier uses the attached device and rappels carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. 11-94. The second involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then tying a big knot close to the anchor with both strands fixing them. All but the last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed strands. The last Soldier unties the knot and rappels carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. RAPPELLING TECHNIQUES 11-95. Different situations call for different rappel attachment techniques. They vary in how much friction they produce, the security in which the rappeller is attached to the rope, and whether they allow the rappeller to go hands free. The consequence of falling determines the type of attachment to the rope. Terrain severity determines how much friction is required to control descent. Whether or not other tasks need to be conducted mid-rappel determines the need for a hands-free brake. 11-96. During rappelling, the body generally forms an L-shape with the feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and buttocks parallel to

to control descent. Whether or not other tasks need to be conducted mid-rappel determines the need for a hands-free brake. 11-96. During rappelling, the body generally forms an L-shape with the feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and buttocks parallel to the ground. When carrying equipment or additional weight, a modified L-shape is used with the legs slightly lower than the buttocks to compensate for the additional weight. The rappeller's back is straight. Rappellers never let go of the ropes with their brake hand until the rappel is complete. Rappellers should keep their feet flat against the surface they are rappelling down and their weight fully on the rope throughout the rappel. Hasty Rappel 11-97. The hasty rappel technique is only used on low-angle slopes. Its primary advantages are that it is simple to learn and execute and requires no specialized equipment. However, take care not to underestimate the terrain being negotiated. Application of this technique in terrain that is too steep can have deadly consequences. The level of rappeller surefootedness determines the severity of terrain for which this technique is appropriate. Gloves can be worn to prevent rope burns. 11-98. Facing slightly sideways to the anchor, rappellers place the ropes horizontally across their back, under their armpits, and palm up. The hand nearest to the anchor is the guide hand, and the other is the brake hand. Bending the rope around the body increases friction. (See figure 11-10, page 292.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 291

Chapter 11 11-99. While moving, Soldiers should keep their legs as perpendicular to the slope as possible, leaning into the rope. This increases the security of foot placements and reduces the likelihood of a slip and fall. 11-100. Most often, it is used as a backup for when a more efficient device is lost or forgotten. 11-102. The drawback of using a Munter hitch is that it twists the rope, causing snarl at the bottom that makes future use difficult. An experienced Soldier can separate the strands with the brake hand and counter the twist of the rope as it feeds through the hitch to lessen this effect. Using a figure-eight descender provides a secure attachment to the rappel rope and adequate friction for use in steep-to-vertical terrain. 11-106. The advantage of these is that they work well with both larger diameter ropes and static or low-stretch ropes. The disadvantages are that they are less versatile, heavier, and bulkier than tube-style devices, which serve multiple mountaineering purposes. 11-107. Chapter 11 11-108. Soldiers assume a typical L-shaped position while rappelling and control their rate of descent with the brake strand by slowly feeding slack from below them toward the device. Two hands should be used on the brake strand, positioned in front of the body below the device. Figure 11-12. Figure-eight descender Tube-Style Devices 11-109. Using a tube-style device provides a secure attachment to the rappel rope and adequate friction for use in steep to vertical terrain. 11-110. Most climbing teams use these. The advantages are that they can be used for both belaying and rappelling with one or two ropes. They are compact and lightweight. They do not twist the ropes as much as figure-eight descenders. The disadvantages are that they do not work as smoothly when used with static or low-stretch ropes due to the more tightly woven rope sheath and stiffer feel. Using an extension moves the rappel device away from the body. This makes it easier to keep two hands on the brake strands. It also reduces the chance of straps or clothing from being caught in the device and stopping rope from feeding through it. This results in the rappeller becoming stuck on the rope, unable to descend, and requires advanced skills to fix. Wearing bulky cold-weather clothing or tactical load-bearing harnesses increase the likelihood of this occurring. Extending the device allows for the use of a hands-free backup. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 295

Chapter 11 11-114. To extend a device, create an extension by girth hitching a sling to the harness. Insert the rappel ropes into the device as described above and clip them into the extension with a locking carabiner. A basket hitch can also be used to create a shorter extension. Under most circumstances, it is recommended to use an extension when rappelling in mountainous terrain because it makes controlling descent easier and less fatiguing to the core when heavy loads are carried. Rappels using the Munter hitch technique cannot be extended. Hands-Free Backup 11-115. A hands-free backup is a rigging technique, involving friction hitches or mechanical devices that prevent a load from falling should control of a brake strand be lost. To establish a hands-free backup, tie an autoblock around the rappel ropes below the device, and attach it to the climber's harness with a locking carabiner. (See figure 11-15, page 300.) Any time an autoblock is used, it must be tested to ensure it grabs before starting the rappel. If it does not, more wraps should be added until it does. 11-116. This allows Soldiers to perform other tasks mid-rappel. The most common example is the first rappeller needing

be tested to ensure it grabs before starting the rappel. If it does not, more wraps should be added until it does. 11-116. This allows Soldiers to perform other tasks mid-rappel. The most common example is the first rappeller needing to untangle the rope on the way down. During rappelling, Soldiers must prevent the autoblock from engaging and stopping their downward progress with one hand while the other feeds rope to the device. To engage the autoblock, the Soldier ceases minding the autoblock and it will engage, forcing the rappel rope into the brake position. When Soldiers are ready to continue rappelling, they resume control of the brake strands with both hands and disengage the autoblock. Descent can then continue. 11-117. Using an autoblock can provide a backup in case Soldier drops the brake strand. However, it is not the best back-up technique for large groups of rappellers to use given the additional time it takes to establish, manage, and untie from the rope. Rucksack Support 11-118. The fireman's belay can be used to prevent rappellers from falling should they lose control of the brake strand. This technique involves a Soldier loosely holding the rappel rope and watching the rappeller from the bottom. If the rappeller falls, the Soldier pulls on the rope hard. This forces the device to brake and stop the rappeller's fall. When the rappeller regains footing and control of the brake strand, tension is released, allowing them to continue rappelling. Chapter 11 Duties and Responsibilities of the Rappel Site Supervisor 11-122. An experienced mountaineer should be overall in charge of any movement on a rope system. This person ensures safety checks are completed and that there is a plan for the flow of personnel onto and off the system and is the one responsible for the entire event. 11-123. Duties of rappel site supervisors are as follows: * Ensures that the anchors are sound, and the knots are properly tied. * Ensures that loose rock and debris are cleared from the loading platform. * Allows only one Soldier per rappel point on the loading platform at a time and ensures that the rappel point is run orderly. * Ensures that each Soldier is properly prepared for the rappel: helmet with chinstrap fastened and harness or rappel seat is correct (if required). They ensure that the rappeller is hooked up to the rope correctly and is aware of the proper braking position. * Ensures that the proper signals or commands are used. * Dispatches each Soldier down the rope. * Ensures the ropes will pull nicely when the rappel is retrieved; gets the joining knot past the edge, if necessary. *

position. * Ensures that the proper signals or commands are used. * Dispatches each Soldier down the rope. * Ensures the ropes will pull nicely when the rappel is retrieved; gets the joining knot past the edge, if necessary. * Ensures safety lines or personal safeties for rappel site personnel are established and Soldiers remain clipped to them when necessary. Communication 11-124. Radio communication from the top to the bottom should be used to ensure all ropes touch the ground and someone is providing a fireman's belay before the rappeller commits to the rappel. 11-125. Loud voice commands for anything other than warning of falling objects should be discouraged, as they are unnecessary and tactically inappropriate. However, if they are used in training, they should be clear, concise, and understood by all participants. 11-126. Chapter 12 Hauling and Lowering Techniques Mountain warfare requires moving Soldiers, weapons, and equipment up, over, and down steep, rugged terrain. It is vital that Soldiers understand the principles and fundamental concepts of hauling and lowering heavy loads both efficiently and safely. SECTION I - HAULING TECHNIQUES 12-1. Mountain operations involve many situations that require hauling systems. A hauling system is a technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that generates increased mechanical advantage (MA) and captures progress. Properly using hauling systems allows Soldiers to move heavy loads through terrain obstacles that would have been impossible to overcome otherwise. Common situations requiring these systems are equipment recovery, resupply, and rescue operations. Choosing the right system for a given situation requires understanding the principles of MA, categories of systems, and solid judgement. MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE 12-2. A mechanical advantage is a reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary

the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary to move a load vertically. This makes hauling heavy loads easier. When choosing and constructing a hauling system, the goal is to use the lowest level of MA to move the load. As MA increases, efficiency and load sensitivity decrease. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches a surface (including the edge of the cliff), moves through carabiners or pulleys, and rubs on itself in the system. Load sensitivity is the ability of the Soldier pulling on the rope to feel what is happening to the load on the end of the rope. For example, a Soldier pulling a heavy load up a slope by hand will know immediately if the load becomes stuck on an obstacle. However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time,

However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time, materials, and personnel to construct and operate. The intent is not to make easy work of moving the load. The lowest level of MA is desired to maximize load sensitivity, efficiency, and time. 12-3. The more MA a rope system produces, the less efficient it will be. For example, a Soldier operating a 5:1 system only needs to exert 1/5 of the pulling force to move the load. However, that Soldier will need to pull 5 feet of rope through the system for the load to move 1 foot. A balance between work and efficiency must be achieved when selecting an appropriate MA for a given situation. HAULING SYSTEM COMPONENTS 12-4. The hauling system has five basic components. Understanding how they work to move the load together (see the list below) allows Soldiers to achieve greater efficiency during hauling: * Anchors-the anchors required for hauling a heavy load must be unquestionable (see chapter 9). TECHNIQUES TO REDUCE FRICTION 12-13. Friction reduces efficiency of rope movement and can drastically reduce MA. It is important to identify points of friction within the system and strive to reduce them. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches hardware. Friction can be minimized by using pulleys. Pulleys are used to change direction in rope systems. Pulleys should be small, lightweight, and rated for mountaineering applications. They should accommodate the largest diameter of rope being used. Pulleys are made with several bearings, different-sized sheaves (wheels), and metal alloy side plates. (See figure 12-8, page 310.) Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than

Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than the rope's diameter to maintain high rope strength. Pulleys with side plates designed to accommodate prusik knots are referred to as prusik minding pulleys. These pulleys are designed with tolerances that allow the ropes to run through them but block the passage of a prusik hitch, preventing it from being caught in the pulley. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 309

Chapter 12 Figure 12-8. Types of pulleys 12-14. Pulleys are estimated to be approximately 90-percent efficient, while carabiners are considered only 60-percent efficient. The difference between a system that uses pulleys at direction changes and the same system that only uses carabiners is significant. If the team only has a few pulleys, they should be used at the direction changes closest to the system's haul strand. Pulleys in these locations will maximize the force put into the system initially and carry 90-percent efficiency farther through the system. 12-15. Friction also occurs where the mainline contacts the edge of the slope or cliff. If a suitable anchor can be found near the edge, this friction point can be minimized. The mainline can be lifted and routed through a high directional at the top of the slope or cliff to reduce rope contact and friction at the edge. (See figure 12-9.) 310 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Hauling and Lowering Techniques SECTION II - LOWERING TECHNIQUES 12-22. A lowering system is a technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain in a controlled fashion using friction hitches or mechanical devices. These sorts of systems are used to control the speed of descent for personnel or equipment using rope. They are an integral part of both highand low-angle rescue. (See chapter 15.) Lowering a victim or a load is always preferred over hauling if the terrain and situation allows. No two situations are identical. Each new situation will dictate which lowering techniques and systems are appropriate. Understanding basic lowering concepts is key to achieving a safe and efficient solution to the problem. LOWERING CONCEPTS 12-23. There are many devices and techniques available depending on the weight of the load. The bottom line for any lowering system is that enough friction must be created to safely control the descent of the load. Different terrain demands different methods of creating friction. When the terrain is steep and broken, selecting a device or technique that provides varying levels of friction is preferred. 12-24. All lowering systems should be closed by securing the free end of the

demands different methods of creating friction. When the terrain is steep and broken, selecting a device or technique that provides varying levels of friction is preferred. 12-24. All lowering systems should be closed by securing the free end of the rope (the end not attached to the load). This prevents lowering the load off the end of the rope if the distance of the lower versus the length of rope is misjudged. 12-25. When lowering Soldiers, a hands-free backup for the system should be used. (See figure 11-15, page 300.) This can be achieved in multiple ways. Hands-free backups provide additional measures of protection against human error and allow the Soldier or team operating the lowering system flexibility while controlling the brake strand. and redirected belay device. TERRAIN FEATURE 12-27. This method involves simply wrapping the rope attached to the load around a natural object, such as a tree or boulder. Chapter 13 Mountain Stream Crossing In 480 BC, Persian King Xerxes constructed a pontoon bridge that spanned a mile and a quarter across the Hellespont. After a previous failure to take Greece, the king weighed the options of either finding alternate routes to the north that added months to his expedition or pinpoint potential water crossing locations for his army. Xerxes insisted on the fastest and most direct route across the Aegean inlet for his 300,000 men. While negotiating the linear obstacle involved massive resources and engineering, it would save precious time for his army to reach their objective. SECTION I - MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS 13-1. A mountain stream crossing is essentially an approach to negotiating a potentially swift and cold waterway that Soldiers may encounter in the mountains. Learning to cross small streams forms a foundation of skills for personnel to manage larger streams and rivers, where consequences could be far more hazardous. 13-2. In an operation involving the crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation

crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation should be conducted economically and with minimal loss of momentum. 13-3. There are limits on the safe use of the techniques discussed in this chapter. Not all mountain rivers or streams will be fordable with these techniques. If a water obstacle is too wide, swift, or deep, an alternate route should be used. It may require using aircraft transport if engineer support is unavailable. Reconnaissance of questionable crossing sites is essential. This chapter covers the techniques for crossing mountain streams that have a depth generally not exceeding waist level. 13-4. Stream crossings should not be taken lightly. Chapter 14 Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Ten percent of the Earth's land mass is covered by glaciers. Glaciers are rivers of ice flowing under the influence of gravity, constantly restructuring the mountains around them. They often provide the best route in otherwise impassable terrain but can contain crevasses and other hazards that can cause injury, death, or compromise a unit's mission. Soldiers operating in glaciated terrain must understand these hazards, be well versed in the fundamentals of glacier travel, and be proficient with crevasse rescue techniques. SECTION I - GLACIER FUNDAMENTALS 14-1. Glaciers can be large enough to cover an entire continent. They may move only inches or hundreds of feet a year. Movement is caused by gravity, slippage over the bedrock, or by the internal flow in the ice. It is important for route planning and risk management to understand glacial features and understand how they form and move. Dismounted movement across glaciers is hazardous; however, glaciers often provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the ice begins to move downhill. The weight of millions of pounds of ice makes a small film of water that acts as a lubricant, enabling it to slide. 14-3. The upper part of the glacier where the annual snow accumulation exceeds the melt is called the accumulation zone. Further down the glacier, the area where melt exceeds accumulation is an area called the ablation zone. The imaginary line between the two zones is known as the firn line. CLASSIFICATION 14-4. There are two classifications of glaciers: alpine glaciers and ice caps. Alpine glaciers form in high mountain bowls. Ice caps can cover thousands of square miles, such as those that cover Greenland and Antarctica. TYPES OF ALPINE GLACIERS 14-5. The following are four types of glaciers: * Valley glacier-resides and flows in a valley. * Cirque glacier-forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl. * Hanging glacier-these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers

These do not advance beyond the bowl. * Hanging glacier-these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers flowing and deteriorating. Chapter 14 GLACIER OBSTACLES 14-6. Units intending to use glaciers for travel routes must be familiar with their hazards and characteristics to ensure safe and efficient movement on them. Failure to identify and prepare for obstacles, which can come in the form of vertical terrain, can slow or prevent movement. Failure to identify and prepare for hazards can result in significant injury or loss of life. 14-7. Glaciers contain many different features that can impede travel. (See figure 14-1.) They are- * Bergschrund-the bergschrund is a giant crevasse found at the upper limit of glacier movement. It is formed where the moving glacier breaks away from the ice cap or snowfield above. The bergschrund can be high and overhanging and can create an obstacle to movement when moving from the valley floor onto the mountainsides. * Crevasses-crevasses are cracks in the glacier caused by irregularities in the bedrock under the glacier as it moves and flows. Crevasses often form where the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction

They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction of the glacier's movement. Crevasses can be 200-feet deep but are normally 40- to 100-feet deep. Crevasses often hinder travel across glaciers. Snow often conceals crevasses, causing possible major falling hazards to Soldiers. Bypassing them can increase travel time and distance. Glaciers are typically large open danger areas and should be treated as such during tactical operations. Units traveling on glaciers are subject to observation from all the surrounding high ground. A capable detachment may be required to provide an overwatch for the force traveling below. EQUIPMENT 14-9. The use of ropes allows Soldiers to move in small rope teams and have some protection from crevasse falls. The type, length, and diameter of ropes selected for this purpose may vary depending upon how steep and heavily crevassed the glacier is. It is also determined by the number of Soldiers per rope team, and whether there are mutually supporting teams. Smaller diameter, lighter weight ropes are generally preferred. HARNESSES 14-11. Chapter 14 ICE AXE AND CRAMPONS 14-12. Ice axes and crampons may be necessary for movement over snow or ice on a glacier but also provide the ability for a Soldier on a rope team to self-arrest to control, stop, and hold the fall of another climber. Ice axes may also be used for snow anchor construction for crevasse rescue. SKIS AND SNOWSHOES 14-13. In deep snow conditions, skis or snowshoes make movement more efficient. They also distribute weight over a greater area when crossing crevasses, which can reduce the likelihood of breaking through a hidden snow bridge. Snowshoes may be more practical than skis for roped glacier travel unless all members of a rope team are skilled skiers. PRUSIKS, SLINGS, AND CORDELETTES 14-14. Short prusik loops, slings, and cordelettes can be used for ascending a rope after a crevasse fall. They are used for belaying rope team members and creating anchors, load transfers, and hauling systems in crevasse rescue. Slings can be used to improvise a chest harness, if necessary, and can be useful to rig the rucksack for removal in the event of a fall. Each Soldier should carry a cordelette, a sling, and a short prusik. SNOW

In some snow conditions, ice axes, skis, and other items may be used to create an anchor. WANDS 14-16. Wands are sticks used as markers and can be utilized in many ways. They can be used to mark the location of known crevasses on frequently used routes or used in pairs forming an X to indicate danger. They can be used while setting up bivouac sites to mark the boundaries of safe areas. They are sometimes useful for whiteout navigation in heavily crevassed terrain. Wands can be made using 4-foot bamboo garden stakes with tape or flagging. OTHER GLACIAL GEAR 14-17. USE OF THE ROPE 14-18. A central question when considering travel over glaciers is whether to use a rope for fall protection. The hazard of hidden crevasses on a glacier varies considerably. In some circumstances, it may be preferable to travel unroped on crevassed glaciers; however, this is not typical. Deciding whether to rope together as a team depends upon the season, mode of travel, snow conditions, and the conditions of the glacier itself. 14-19. Traveling unroped is faster. It makes communication and dissemination of information easier; it can be done with untrained Soldiers. It eliminates the transition times required for tying in and preparing for roped travel. It also allows for movement in tactical formations and a better security posture. 14-20. HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD 14-21. In glaciated terrain, there can be both a risk of falling on steep ground as well as a risk of falling into crevasses. These risks are not managed in the same way. Crevasse hazard is best managed with good route finding and by keeping 8 to 10 meters of rope between Soldiers. Rope teams can usually stop crevasse falls because these occur on low-angled terrain without falling hazard. On flat terrain or soft snow, the arresting Soldiers are not typically at risk of sliding into the crevasse and are often able to stop the fall by slumping in the snow, rather than a full team self-arrest. 14-22. Chapter 14 Figure 14-4. Preparation chest harness, rucksack removal sling for use with prusik ascent ROPE MANAGEMENT 14-33. The rope should be kept extended on a glacier. It should not have unnecessary slack or be taut. Excess slack will cause a Soldier to fall deeper into a crevasse, placing more force on other members of the team and increasing the difficulty of arresting the fall. The falling climber is more likely to hit something or become stuck or wedged. 14-34. A rope with the correct amount of tension lies on the snow with a gentle curve, out of the way of the feet. It can be helpful to hold the rope to the front when traveling downhill and to the rear when traveling uphill. Pace should be adjusted to maintain correct tension in the rope by feel, especially during stops and starts. The Soldier in the lead should set a pace that others can easily follow. 340 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue 14-35. During sharp turns, the rope tends to go slack as the lead Soldier makes a change in the direction of travel, but then it becomes taut as the next Soldier approaches the turn. During turns, team members should adjust pace and keep appropriate tension. New tracks may need to be made outside the leader's footprints to do this. 14-36. As a rope team reaches a rest area or bivouac location, the rope must remain extended until the area has been probed for crevasses. Once it has been deemed safe, the lead member may belay team members into the area by pulling rope through the prusik, with ice axe in hand, ready to self-arrest. Soldiers in the rear may also belay themselves into the location in the same manner. When leaving the location, the same process happens in reverse. (See figure 14-5.) Figure 14-5. Chapter 14 ROUTE FINDING AND CREVASSE DETECTIONS 14-37. Crevasse falls are extremely dangerous, even when traveling roped up with experienced Soldiers. Even when all Soldiers manage the rope well and the fall is stopped immediately, severe injuries can result. Ice axes, crampons, and collapsing snow bridges can cause injuries. Detection and avoidance are the primary skills needed to eliminate the need for crevasse rescue. On heavily crevassed glaciers, it is advisable to use an advanced party to scout and mark the safest route in advance of the main body. This can save hours of wandering, slow progress, and running into dead ends. Once relatively safe routes are established, it can reduce the skill and experience level required of the main body. INFORMATION GATHERING 14-38. Big picture views of the terrain can be very helpful. A maze of crevasses can be analyzed more easily from above than from within. It is a good idea to take digital photos whenever high ground provides a vantage point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even old photographs useful for study. TIMING 14-39. On snow covered and heavily crevassed glaciers, snow bridges are firmer at night or early in the morning. If stable, they can often provide more direct lines of travel. Warmer daytime temperatures can soften these snow bridges, increasing the likelihood of crevasse fall. This may require finding a longer alternative route. 14-40. Be cautious after snowstorms. Fresh snow can fill in and blend in what might otherwise be detectable crevasses. 14-41. Seasonal timing is equally important. Although unit leaders may not have much say in the time of year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface conditions is important. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue ZONES OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION 14-43. Crevasses are formed by tension. Tension is created as glacier ice stretches over rolls in the terrain and where it stretches due to different rates of flow within the glacier. These crevasses form perpendicular to the direction of the stretch. Recognizing where this tension is likely to occur can help with predicting their likely locations when snow fills in or conceals them. Crevasses are more likely at the top of a roll, where the terrain gets steeper and drops away below it. They are also common near the edges of valley glaciers, where additional drag and friction occurs against the valley walls, and the center of the glacier is moving faster. These "marginal" crevasses point toward the center of the glacier at an angle. For this same reason, the centers of glaciers generally have fewer crevasses and are preferred travel routes. 14-44. Compression zones occur where the underlying bedrock flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of

flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of compression can be relatively crevasse-free. Observing these zones and working to link them together are keys to good route finding. SURFACE CLUES 14-45. Clues to locating crevasses below the surface of the snow can be subtle and difficult to recognize, but it is important for determining an appropriate crossing technique. It can also be just as important to recognize similar clues that do not indicate crevasses and to not waste time and effort on long detours. * Sagging-snow covering larger crevasses gradually deforms and sags under its own weight. Early in the process, this may be barely noticeable, but later the outlines of the crevasse become more defined. Sometimes a slight change in sheen or texture can be observed. Other times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change

times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change represents a crevasse. In low visibility or flat light, these can be impossible to recognize. * Nearby crevasses-since crevasses are often found in groups and tend to form parallel to one another, look for other crevasses, patterns, or depressions nearby that have similar orientation. * Parallel cracks-in the case of larger crevasses, parallel thin cracks can sometimes form at the edges of a giant snow bridge. Although these can have the appearance of two narrow crevasses, they can be the boundaries of a single, giant snow bridge. PROBING 14-46. Snow probing in areas that look suspicious can be done using an ice axe. It can identify crevasses, determine its true lip, and investigate the extent, length, and width of a crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a

crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a crevasse, but it can also be a soft snow layer. Probing requires experience to accurately interpret. The short length of an ice axe makes this difficult. Avalanche probes and ski poles with the basket removed are better choices, if available. Probing is also required for determining safe bivouac locations. CROSSING TECHNIQUES 14-47. There are a variety of options and techniques for crossing crevasses, and leaders must understand and be capable of incorporating any combination of them to adapt to the terrain. Rope teams should travel perpendicular to the direction of crevasses to reduce the risk of exposing more than one Soldier at a time. (See figure 14-6, page 344.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 343

Chapter 14 Figure 14-6. Crossing perpendicular to crevasses End Running 14-48. There is no guarantee as to the dependability of snow bridges. Sometimes it is preferable to cross at one end of a crevasse where its width narrows, rather than take a chance with a snow bridge. (See figure 14-7.) With large crevasses, this could lead to traveling a quarter of a mile or more to gain 30 feet of forward progress. In winter or spring, seasonal snow may still cover the narrow ends of a crevasse. What looks like the end of the crevasse might not be its actual end. This assessment can require some judgement. Make a wide swing, probe carefully, and cross at a right angle to the crevasse. 344 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Figure 14-7. End running crevasses Using a Snow Bridge 14-49. When end running is not practical, use snow bridges to cross. (See figure 14-8.) Always attempt to get a look at the crevasse from the side before committing to it, and probe when approaching the lip. The remaining Soldier in the team provides a moving belay by controlling the slack and remaining ready to self-arrest. Once the leader is across, the rest of the team must follow exactly in the leader's footsteps. At this point, the leader controls slack and remains prepared for self-arrest. Prusiks can be used here to manage slack in the rope during this process as well. If there is doubt as to one's ability to stop a fall, a fixed belay must be constructed with a snow or ice anchor. Chapter 14 Jumping 14-50. Only conduct jumping when the gap is short. Running leaps requiring big push offs from suspect crevasse lips and falls can result in serious injury. Jumping should not be attempted unless there are no other options. Enough slack must be provided for the jumper to clear the crevasse without question. Be wary of catching a crampon and use common sense. Climbing into the Crevasse 14-51. Occasionally, it may be practical to climb down into a shallow crevasse and climb back out the other side. Standard belay techniques (see chapter 10) should be used. Be especially aware of bottoms that appear solid but are not. Echelon Formation 14-52. When it is impractical to travel perpendicular to existing crevasses and Soldiers must travel parallel, the echelon formation can be used. (See figure 14-9.) This keeps team members still to the rear but offset slightly to the side. This provides an alternative to following the leader's tracks in a single-file line. This should only be used on heavily crevassed sections where all crevasses are visible and there is very little risk of falling into a hidden one. Figure 14-9. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue CREVASSE FALL CONSIDERATIONS 14-54. Mutually supporting rope teams should have a minimum of one Soldier per team who is trained in crevasse rescue. This will ensure that rescue capability can always be provided, even when the more experienced member of another rope team is the one to fall in. Two trained Soldiers are necessary in rope teams traveling independently, away from supporting teams. 14-55. Crevasse falls are rarely dramatic and sudden falls that rip team members off their feet and result in someone dangling down inside an abyss. In fact, most crevasse falls involve breaking through a snow bridge but falling no further than waste deep, and with minimal force exerted on team members. Despite this, Soldiers must be trained to deal with more severe falls and be able to adapt and adjust to a variety of circumstances. Options for crevasse rescue involve an abundance of variables. They depend largely upon the breakdown of rope teams, the number of Soldiers per rope, conditions of the glacier, and specific equipment carried. A comprehensive and detailed description of crevasse rescue techniques is well beyond the scope of this publication. Instead, the steps and decision process typically used

Instead, the steps and decision process typically used for a three-person rope team are described below. STEPS TO TAKE FOR CREVASSE FALL 14-56. The following steps should be considered in the event of a crevasse fall with a three-person rope team. STOP THE FALL 14-57. Stop the fall immediately. Some falls may be barely noticeable, while others may require dropping into the self-arrest position in the opposite direction. Stopping falls on firm surfaces can be more difficult than soft ones. Once the fall is arrested, both rescuers should kick crampon points into the snow to establish a strong, stable position to prevent the victim from slipping any further. Communication can often be made with the victim at this point. In circumstances where Soldiers have only fallen a few feet or are stuck in the snow bridge, they may be able to climb out unassisted. If a Soldier is not able to quickly self-recover, then the following steps must be taken. (See figure 14-10, page 348.) 26 November 2025
