Chapter 14 Figure 14-10. Stopping a crevasse fall CONSTRUCT AN ANCHOR AND TRANSFER THE LOAD 14-58. When another rope team is available, then they can construct an anchor and help the team transfer the load of the fallen Soldier onto it. (See figure 14-11.) Otherwise, the Soldier on the opposite end is usually the one to complete this step. End Soldiers slowly get out of the self-arrest, making sure that middle Soldiers can still hold the weight. End Soldiers establish an anchor (see chapter 9 for snow and ice anchors) below the middle climber and towards the crevasse. They attach a prusik to the loaded rope and clip it to the anchor with a locking carabiner. If there is limited distance between the middle climber and the crevasse lip, the anchor can be constructed above the middle climber. In this case, the slack rope itself, between the middle and end climber can be used to attach directly to the anchor. 348 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue 14-59. Next, the end Soldiers get back into the self-arrest position to back up middle Soldiers as they transfer the weight of fallen Soldiers onto this prusik. Once pressure is relieved from middle Soldiers, it is common for them to continue backing up this anchor while the end climber improves it or constructs additional components. This anchor must be unquestionably strong, as it may be used to haul the Soldier out. The prusik should also be backed up with a suitable knot clipped to the anchor. Figure 14-11. Construct the anchor and transfer the load COMMUNICATE WITH THE FALLEN CLIMBER AND MAKE A PLAN 14-60. To make a clear assessment and develop a plan, it is best to approach the edge of the crevasse where the fallen Soldier can be seen and heard. This can be done by one of the team members using a safety prusik attached to the unweighted portion of the rope. Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded

Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded rope can often become entrenched into the lip of the crevasse, complicating rescue options. This may be a good time to pad underneath the rope to prevent this from becoming worse with an ice axe shaft, foam pad, or rucksack slid underneath the rope as close to the edge as can be reached. This can take some work, and items used for padding should be anchored so that it cannot fall into the crevasse. Various options for rescue are described below. Self-Rescue 14-61. Self-rescue can be achieved by the fallen climber ascending the rope itself using a prusik ascent (see paragraphs 11-39 through 11-49, pages 282 through 284) or other techniques discussed in chapter 11 and is also shown in figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope

figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope is also particularly helpful for staying upright. Assistance from team members may be required to surmount the crevasse lip. The method does not work if the fallen Soldier sustained significant injuries. Belay 14-62. Belays may be a fast, easy option when crampons and ice axes can be used to climb out of the hole, especially if or when the rope is too entrenched in the crevasse lip to prusik out. The remaining free end of the rope can be passed down to the fallen climber to tie into the harness with, while a team member above creates a belay at the anchor. Again, if the fallen Soldier is injured, this method may not be possible. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 349

Chapter 14 Haul 14-63. If none of the above options are viable, a more complex solution of hauling the fallen climber out will be needed. HAULING 14-64. Hauling techniques used for MA described in chapter 12 may be used for hauling; however, there are circumstances specific to working with crevasses that must be considered. Direct Haul 14-65. This refers to hauling systems constructed on the fallen climber's weighted strand of rope. A common example is the 3:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-4, page 307.) This is constructed by untying the backup knot behind the prusik and using this remaining rope to construct the system. A disadvantage to the direct haul is that it does not work if the rope is entrenched in the crevasse lip. This method is also impractical if there are knots tied in the weighted rope to help hold the crevasse fall. (See figure 14-12.) Figure 14-12. Direct haul using a 3:1 hauling system 350 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Drop Loop 14-66. Drop loops refer to hauling systems that use a bight of rope sent down and attach to the fallen climber's harness, independent of the climber's weighted strand. (See figure 14-13.) An example is the 2:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-3, page 307.) This is often the preferred method because the crevasse lip can be padded prior to hauling and because the victim can often assist by pulling on the strand opposite the haul strand. Drop-loop hauls do require victims to clip the bight of rope into the harness, so in the case of an unconscious victim, this step may need to be done by first rappelling to them then re-ascending. Drop-loop systems can be performed using the remainder of the rope or by a separate rope team utilizing a different rope altogether. Progress must still be captured during the haul for safety. This may be done by pulling rope through the prusik on the original tensioned rope. Figure 14-13. Drop-loop rescue system (2:1) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 351

Chapter 14 SECTION IV - TRAINING 14-67. Even when mutually supporting rope teams are used, good route finding, and crevasse detection skills are critical. Every rope team must have at least one Soldier with solid crevasse rescue skills. Commanders cannot just hope for seasonally low-risk conditions, nor can they rely solely on advanced parties or recon teams to consistently find routes that are passable without the need for ropes. A lack of expertise can leave units with a large capability gap. 14-68. Training and experience in glacier travel are most productive when conducted on glaciers. Most glaciated terrain in the lower 48 states is in the Pacific Northwest. The high cost of travel and time commitments to access them make training plans difficult for units to execute. Most of those glaciers involve acquiring climbing permits. It can take the better part of a training day for the approach on foot to these higher elevations; any training would typically involve a bivouac. This makes it inconvenient even for units located at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington. Ambitious commanders, however, might utilize these or other glaciated terrain in Alaska, Europe, or elsewhere, to create training events that combine glacier experience with other aspects

Ambitious commanders, however, might utilize these or other glaciated terrain in Alaska, Europe, or elsewhere, to create training events that combine glacier experience with other aspects of mountain warfare. 14-69. In the absence of glaciated terrain, units can still conduct simulated training exercises focusing on the basic strategies for roping up and preparing individual and team equipment. Crevasse rescue skills can be rehearsed using short sections of steep terrain. This should be conducted in locations without serious falling hazard, and back-up ropes or belays should be considered while techniques are being learned. Having a few unit members with advanced level training will improve the quality and outcomes of this training. 352 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Chapter 15 Mountain Rescue and Evacuation A unit's capability to conduct mountain rescue and evacuation is a critical part of mountain operations. Swift and efficient rescue can mean the difference between success and failure of a mission or even the survival of a casualty. In mountainous terrain, even relatively minor injuries may require evacuation. The type of injury, distance to be moved, terrain, training level of the team, and litter capabilities determine the evacuation technique chosen. Air evacuation is preferred. However, the weather, tactical situation, or operational ceiling of the aircraft may make this impossible. Therefore, it is imperative that all personnel are trained in mountain evacuation techniques and are self-sufficient. Casualties should be triaged before evacuation. The most experienced medical personnel available perform triage (physician, physician's assistant, or medic). SECTION I - RESCUE OPERATIONS 15-1. Every commander should have a MEDEVAC plan before undertaking an operation. This plan should have dedicated assets (primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency) in place so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting

so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting winds reduce the ability of fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft to assist in operations. Therefore, relying solely on aircraft or specialized equipment is a poor substitute for careful planning. 15-2. The two types of rescue operations encountered by units operating in mountainous environments are deliberate and improvised. DELIBERATE 15-3. Deliberate rescue is when the mission objective itself is a rescue operation, thus allowing time for focused planning and the use of specialized rescue specific equipment. IMPROVISED 15-4. Improvised rescue situations are encountered when a casualty is sustained during normal operations and conducting a rescue was not the intended objective. Even improvised rescue operations should be practiced and rehearsed to minimize the negative effects on mission capability. All operations should have a CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a

CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a potential rescue. PLANNING 15-5. The rescue tasks must be identified by obtaining the following information: * Number of casualties by precedence (urgent, priority, routine, convenience). * Number of casualties by type (litter or ambulatory) and the nature of their injuries. * Terrain features and with respect to the location of the casualties. * Tactical situation. * Any assets available to aid in security, rescue, treatment, and evacuation. * If treatment can be provided at the scene or if the casualty requires movement to a safer location. * Additional personnel or equipment required for the rescue operation. * Any circumstances that may require specialized skills. * Weather conditions. * Difficulty of the terrain. * Time available. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 353

Chapter 15 15-6. Route selection when planning mountain CASEVAC often depends upon technical capabilities. In some cases, trained personnel and equipment available for low- or high-angle rescue may allow for safer, less physically demanding operations. A lack of these resources and capabilities may require traveling longer distances around steeper terrain, greatly increasing the burden on rescuers. CONSIDERATIONS 15-7. Time considerations can cause a leader to compromise planning stages or treatment (beyond first aid). Make a realistic estimate of time available as quickly as possible to determine the action time remaining. The key elements are the casualty's condition and ability to endure the environment. Time available is a balance between these conditions and the resources and personnel available. 15-8. There are many additional considerations for the rescue team during deliberate rescue: * Typically, team members must distribute and carry all equipment, including hot food and drinks, stoves, sleeping bags, bivouac equipment, warm clothes, ropes, and stretchers. * Evacuation routes often require extensive preparation and can involve establishing anchor points, belays, fixed ropes, lowers, and raises. * Altitude and visibility can greatly affect the team as well as the casualty. Maximum use of secure, reliable trails or roads is essential. * Protection

extensive preparation and can involve establishing anchor points, belays, fixed ropes, lowers, and raises. * Altitude and visibility can greatly affect the team as well as the casualty. Maximum use of secure, reliable trails or roads is essential. * Protection from the elements, such as blankets, tarps, warming layers and rain gear, can be vital. Even a mild rain can complicate an otherwise simple rescue. In higher altitudes, extreme cold or strong winds can greatly increase the rescue's time and complexity. GENERAL STEPS 15-9. Regardless of whether a rescue is deliberate or improvised, the following steps must be taken upon arrival at the rescue site to accomplish a safe and efficient rescue operation: * Assume command-one person and one person only is in charge. * Scene safety-prevent further injuries to the casualty and to others. Explore all options for casualty access prior to committing to one. Use reasonable care in reaching the casualty. Rescuers must not become casualties. * Immediately ensure the casualty has an open airway, control serious bleeding, and protect the casualty from further harm and from environmental hazards. If the casualty is unconscious, continually monitor for a pulse. * Do not move the casualty until determining the

ensure the casualty has an open airway, control serious bleeding, and protect the casualty from further harm and from environmental hazards. If the casualty is unconscious, continually monitor for a pulse. * Do not move the casualty until determining the extent of injuries unless necessary to prevent further injury or if the casualty is in a dangerous or exposed location. * Do nothing more until the situation has been thoroughly considered. Resist the urge for action. Speed is less important than correct actions and decision making. The decisions made on scene drive the rest of the rescue (for example, casualty rigging, packaging, route selection, anchors, and rope systems). * Decide whether to evacuate with available resources or to send or call for help. Speed in getting to the next level of care must be balanced against the probability of further injury. This is especially crucial if working with inexperienced personnel, insufficient equipment, or terrain or weather hazards. * When the evacuation route is long and arduous, a series of litter relay points or stations should be established, if possible. These help to manage the welfare of both the casualty and the rescue team. These stations should be staffed with the

evacuation route is long and arduous, a series of litter relay points or stations should be established, if possible. These help to manage the welfare of both the casualty and the rescue team. These stations should be staffed with the medical personnel and equipment necessary to provide proper treatment. * Helicopters or heated vehicles, if available, should be used for evacuation. While the use of aircraft or vehicles is preferred and can expedite a rescue operation, evacuation of a seriously wounded Soldier should never be delayed awaiting aircraft, vehicle, or a change in weather. SPECIALIZED TRAINING 15-10. Rescue team members must receive basic instruction in military mountaineering and first aid, prior to any training and rehearsals for mountain rescue and evacuation. Individual mobility skills, knowledge of knots and basic rope systems, and the ability to sustain and protect themselves from the environment are 354 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation essential. Once formal evacuation training has been received, proficiency can be maintained by periodic integration with other concurrent training exercises. Scenarios that require simple casualty movement techniques, with and without litters, as well as low-angle slope evacuations (see section II) can easily be created. Scenarios are added when time becomes available during or following other training exercises. These opportunities allow commanders to quickly evaluate a unit's preparedness to carry out basic rescues if needed, refresh level 1 skills, and help to reinforce unit teamwork and problem solving. Basic military mountaineers, at a minimum, should oversee this training. Medical personnel should be present. Rescues in complex 4th- and 5th-class terrain, whether real or simulated, require advanced-level training and skills, and they must be led by level 2 and level 3 mountaineers. PROLONGED FIELD CARE 15-11. The mountain environment is defined by austere and remote conditions. This environment, combined with the difficulty of patient movement, creates situations that can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training

can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training may be required to perform beyond their skillset. Specific training should be conducted to prepare medical and nonmedical personnel for prolonged field care situations. Tactical combat casualty care uses protocols aimed primarily at preventing mortality in the first few hours of treatment, prior to arrival at surgical resuscitative care. However, patients in the mountains lacking fast and immediate evacuation are often at risk for complications, such as sepsis, multi-organ system failure, respiratory compromise, and other serious conditions. Prolonged field care begins with the sound principles of tactical combat casualty care, but when care is extended over hours or days, treatment must continuously be re-evaluated. Diligence is necessary to minimize the effect of potentially harmful interventions and to prevent, recognize, and treat conditions that may develop over time. 15-13. Critical patients ultimately require care in a hospital with surgery, blood products, an intensive care unit, and advanced imaging. A combination of rescue skills training and prolonged field care skills are necessary

treat conditions that may develop over time. 15-13. Critical patients ultimately require care in a hospital with surgery, blood products, an intensive care unit, and advanced imaging. A combination of rescue skills training and prolonged field care skills are necessary to make this possible. SECTION II - CASUALTY MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES 15-14. Casualties in the mountains can be moved and transported in a variety of ways, from simple manual field carries to high-angle evacuations using litters and complex rope systems. The type of injury, distance to be moved, time available, and resources will determine the best technique for a given situation. MOVING CASUALTIES WITHOUT LITTERS 15-15. There are varieties of circumstances where casualties may move, be moved, or be carried without the use of litters. This could be a result of sustaining relatively minor injuries, not having a litter available, or not having the available personnel for litter transport. Alternatively, these could involve moving a casualty in technical terrain that is not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. A rescuer close behind can help in difficult terrain. Have team members ahead to select

not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. A rescuer close behind can help in difficult terrain. Have team members ahead to select the easiest route and remove loose branches and other obstacles. Ski poles may be helpful if they are available. In situations where the casualty cannot walk, simple techniques described in the Soldier's Manual of Common Tasks (fireman's carry, two-hand, four-hand, saddleback, piggyback, pistol belt, and poncho litter) may be useful. Coil the length of rope using the mountain coil technique, sizing the loops to fit from the casualty's armpits to crotch, and then separate the coil in half to form a pair of loops. Make slits in the sides of a large rucksack so the casualty can step into it as though it were a pair of shorts. Then the carrier wears the backpack as usual. Chapter 15 Figure 15-3. Tandem rappel rigging ROPED MOVEMENTS 15-20. Casualties can also be placed in a seat or improvised harness and lowered or hauled through steep terrain using the techniques described in chapter 12. This may be done with ambulatory patients or may be necessary in situations where an injured Soldier must be moved from a cliff to an alternate location where packaging in a litter is more easily accomplished. This may require considerable assistance from rescuers or other Soldiers. It should only be attempted when necessary and after any immediate life-threatening injuries have been treated. Remember the more complex the technical rope systems become, the more time consuming they tend to be, increasing exposure and vulnerability to enemy attack. MOVING CASUALTIES IN LITTERS 15-21. Usually, casualties with significant injuries in the mountains need to be evacuated with the use of a litter. Several types of litters are available for transporting casualties in rough terrain. 358 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation MANUFACTURED LITTERS 15-22. The following litters are readily available to mountaineering units: * The poleless, nonrigid litter is lightweight and readily available but is the least favored litter. It does little to protect the patient's injuries and is not appropriate for attachment to any rope system. * The standard collapsible litter is readily available in all units and may be rigged for movement over rough mountainous terrain. However, it is not suitable for carry as a contingency litter due to its bulk and weight. * A rigid, metal-framed, basket-style litter that is rated for hoist operations is very well-suited for moving casualties through mountainous environments. These litters provide excellent patient protection and spinal immobilization, and when rigged properly, can readily attach to a variety of technical rope systems. The drawbacks to this type of litter are that it is heavy and is not designed to slide over surfaces. A single-wheel attachment is available, which vastly increases the efficiency of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried. * The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic litter that can also be

the efficiency of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried. * The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic litter that can also be rigged to meet rating requirements for hoist operations. The most commonly issued and used version in mountaineering is the rescue litter, which provides excellent patient support and protection. This is the preferred litter for mountain operations due to its versatility and relatively low weight. However, it is not a spinal immobilization device. A backboard must be used with this system for patients who have injuries to the shoulder area. This system will accommodate long and short backboards, scoop stretchers, and most other immobilization equipment. IMPROVISED LITTERS 15-23. Litters can be improvised in the field using several techniques, but all of them require construction materials and time, generally offer less patient protection, and are more prone to breakage. 15-24. Litters can be made by securing poles inside blankets, tarps, ponchos, jackets, shirts, sacks, or bags. Poles can be improvised from strong branches, tent supports, skis, and other similar items. 15-25. If poles cannot be found, a large item, such as a

be made by securing poles inside blankets, tarps, ponchos, jackets, shirts, sacks, or bags. Poles can be improvised from strong branches, tent supports, skis, and other similar items. 15-25. If poles cannot be found, a large item, such as a blanket, can be rolled from both sides toward the center. Then the rolls can be used to obtain a firm grip to carry the casualty. If a poncho is used, the hood must be up and under the victim, not dragging on the ground. PATIENT PACKAGING 15-26. Casualties must be packaged and secured to litters before movement in rough terrain. Proper packaging should achieve stabilization, immobilization, protection from hypothermia, and preparation for transport. Physically strapping a person into a litter is relatively easy but making it comfortable and effective can be a challenge. The needs of litter bound casualties are great and should not be overlooked or underestimated. The decisions made during initial packaging will affect the physical and mental outcomes for the casualty in the end. 15-27. In severely uneven terrain, such as talus or boulder fields, the pass-through technique can make movement safer for both the casualty and rescuers, provided extra personnel are available. To conduct the pass-through technique, simply have extra litter bearers take up static positions in the terrain ahead of the litter and as close to one another as possible. High-angle rescue generally refers to roped evacuations down steep cliffs and 5th-class terrain. High-angle rescue requires formal training, experience, excellent judgement, and good technical problem-solving skills. It often requires a substantial amount of time. Only level 2 and 3 military mountaineers should only conduct high-angle rescue, when necessary. There are often many variables involved in high-angle rescue, and thus, there is no prescriptive set way to deal with the many challenges that can be encountered. Because a combination of skills and techniques may ultimately be required, including climbing techniques, belays, rappels, hauling and lowering methods, or even the use of high lines, a comprehensive focus is well beyond the scope of this training circular. Rather, this section will focus on some of the fundamental principles and commonly used tools and techniques. LITTER RIGGING 15-48. Whether a rescue litter or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be rigged for a vertical orientation the same as

or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be rigged for a vertical orientation the same as described for lower-angle evacuations. In many cases, it is ideal to package the casualty in a manufactured or improvised harness. This allows the harness to connect to the rope system independently of the attachment to the litter itself. This can also be achieved with webbing using a variety of techniques. Horizontal Orientation 15-49. Horizontal orientation of the litter is often used in cases where the nature of the injury makes vertical orientation unsuitable, such as spinal, pelvic, and lower leg injuries. (See figure 15-8.) Severely hypothermic and cardiac patients should also be kept as horizontal as possible during transport. The rescue litter comes with two hoist straps that can be used for this. In the case of a similar metal basket litter, cordage or webbing can be rigged to connect the four corners to a single midline attachment point. (See figure 15-9.) Ensure the head end of the litter is slightly higher than the foot end, about 6 inches when

basket litter, cordage or webbing can be rigged to connect the four corners to a single midline attachment point. (See figure 15-9.) Ensure the head end of the litter is slightly higher than the foot end, about 6 inches when unloaded. Use locking carabiners and ensure that all carabiners used in the rigging are oriented correctly. It is easy to create a dangerous situation by cross-loading carabiners. 364 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Vertical litter orientation is often preferred as it can make for a simpler and more fluid edge transition. It is also lower profile, protects the patient better from rockfall and other hazards, and does not require a change in rope attachment point when transitioning to or from low-angle terrain. However, this method can be unsuitable for casualties with spinal, pelvic, and some lower leg injuries and requires securing the patient in such a way to minimize movement in the litter once evacuation begins. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 365

Chapter 15 ROPE SELECTION 15-51. Rope rescue systems should meet the industry standard 10:1 static system safety factor (SSSF). Calculate the SSSF by first determining the force created by the rescue load. Each person attached to the system is estimated to create 1 kN. Therefore, one casualty and one rescuer are estimated to be a 2-kN load. For a 2-kN load, all components of the rescue system must be rated to 20-kN breaking strength to meet the 10:1 SSSF requirement. In this case, ropes would require a minimum breaking strength of around 30 kN to account for an estimated 1/3 strength loss when knots are tied into the rope. Most static kernmantle ropes 11 mm in diameter meet this 30 kN threshold. However, for mountain rescue operations, it is much more practical to use lighter weight ropes that can more easily be carried, allow for faster response times, and function better with other components of the mountaineering kits. These may have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of

have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of edge abrasion issues. These ropes should be static (low stretch) and should have a minimum diameter of 9.5 mm and a minimum breaking strength of 26 kN. 15-52. Rescues can be carried out using single or tandem rope systems. Single Rope 15-53. Single rope technique, much like that described for use with low-angle rescue, is typically simpler to construct and operate, and generally requires less equipment overall. However, it does not include redundancy for system or rope failure. Equipment breakage or human error can have catastrophic results. Consider using this technique only when there is no prominent edge transition, no sharp rock edges on the pitch, and time and resources are limited. Tandem Rope 15-54. Tandem rope technique is more complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult

complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult edge transitions due to the potential for high-peak forces in the event of failure, sharp rock edges, or when there is limited team experience regarding the rigging of anchors and lowering or belay systems. 15-55. Tandem rope technique uses two separate ropes referred to as the main line and the belay line. Each rope system requires a separate anchor. The main line is used to haul or lower the litter, and the belay line is there in case of main line failure. 15-56. The two ropes are connected to the litter attachment point with interlocking long tailed bowlines. (See figure 15-10.) While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will be significant due to the short amount of rope available to absorb the force, and the static nature of all the system components. Two prusiks, preferably made from 7- or 8-mm nylon static utility cord are tied approximately 2-inches apart on the belay line. Precise commands and singular control are necessary for safe operations. All commands should originate either with the team leader, control, or, in some cases, the edge safety. Chapter 16 Rope Bridges Operations in mountainous terrain often encounter obstacles, such as fast flowing water, ravines, or rock fields. Well-trained mountaineers can exploit this terrain with the use of rope bridges and high lines. These allow units to take the terrain out of the equation by using a rope suspended in the air to cross the obstacle. High lines are a type of rope bridge. The two terms are often used synonymously, and the techniques are relatively interchangeable; however, for the purposes of this training circular, we will refer to rope bridges when used for assisting personnel for river crossings and the term "high lines" to denote rope installations used to span longer or higher gaps in terrain. SECTION I - TECHNIQUES 16-1. A rope bridge is a rope tensioned between two anchors and suspended off the ground to assist units with crossing rivers. These are sometimes necessary in situations with swift and dangerous currents or very cold water, where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are

where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are fixed and potentially split by the river obstacle for prolonged periods. This can put them at a significant tactical disadvantage. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more VDA-crossing considerations.) CONSTRUCTION 16-3. The rope bridge is constructed using a static rope. The rope is anchored on the far side of the obstacle in the same manner as described for using handlines in paragraphs 13-26 through 13-29, page 327. It is then tensioned and anchored on the near side of the obstacle. A rope bridge may be built many ways depending upon the tactical situation and area to be crossed. However, all rope bridges share common safety principles for construction and use. Rope bridges must be tensioned as low as practical on the anchor while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are

while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are multiple ways to apply tension to a rope. The method selected depends on the length of the bridge, equipment available, personnel available, and time. Regardless of the method used, the principle remains the same; apply just enough tension to facilitate ease of crossing through the terrain. WARNING Ropes must not be overtensioned. An overtensioned rope is in its weakest state, and the system can apply exponential forces during use. Critical failures can occur with overtensioned ropes. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 371

The benefit of hand tensioning the rope is that it is the fastest way to get the rope tight. The limitation is that if the rope bridge span is long, it may not be possible to apply adequate tension to the rope using this method. Adequate tension may require more personnel than units have available. TRANSPORT TIGHTENING SYSTEM 16-7. WARNING No more than four personnel should be used to tighten the rope when a simple 3:1 or a transport tightening system is used to apply tension. Using more personnel can overtighten the rope and bring the rope critically close to failure. REDUNDANCY 16-13. A rope bridge constructed with a single rope has the risk of critical failure due to cutting and lacks redundancy. A redundancy (in rigging) is the condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge

failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge that is high off the ground, and a dry river crossing where a separate belay rope is not used. If two ropes are used, they should be as close as possible so that a single carabiner can be clipped to both lines. An individual would attach to both ropes when crossing, thus having a backup in case of failure. All wet crossing techniques using handlines are covered in chapter 13. Methods of dry crossings using rope bridges is determined by several factors: * The load being transported on the rope bridge (such as personnel, equipment, and litter). * The risk of the terrain (such as fast-moving water and catastrophic falls). * The angle of the rope bridge (such as level, ascending, and descending). * Equipment available (such as extra ropes, harnesses, and rigging equipment). 16-15.
